name: North Ridge
approach: Start at the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft), reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road, Wolf Creek Road and a gravel Forest Service road to its end. Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek and then rolls up the valley through forest heavily burned in 2021, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on; it is a long, up-and-down walk of about 10 miles to Gardner Meadows at the end of the trail, where most parties camp. From one of the last campsites, a faint path crosses Wolf Creek and continues up the far side toward Abernathy Lake; it is an old, abandoned trail that disappears in the old burn, so the rest is off-trail. Stay high above Abernathy Lake rather than dropping to it, and make a rising traverse into the upper basin with a small tarn, where the remains of an old cabin and mining equipment mark the old mining camp; a stream just below the tarn is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising to the main north ridge, which has a few exposed class 3 moves, then follow a short boot path along the crest past more mining remains. The path fades past the mine, and the rest is class 2-3 scrambling on boulders and scree to the summit. The upper slopes face south and are normally snow-free from about early July; earlier, firm snow can make the loose talus easier at the cost of carrying an axe.
descent: Abernathy Peak's North Ridge is a scramble, not a technical roped climb, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this route — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the class 3 ridge crest north back toward the top of the spur ridge (the route's crux terrain, with a couple of noticeably 'intense' exposed spots — face in and downclimb deliberately here, since the same loose, eroded rock that's manageable going up is more consequential coming down). From there, most parties drop down the scree slope toward the tarn with the old mining camp rather than reversing the spur ridge; an old path leaves the crest and descends to the upper lake. From the tarn, retrace the rough off-trail line past Abernathy Lake back to Gardner Meadows and follow the Wolf Creek Trail out to the trailhead. This is a 0-rappel walk-off/downclimb in normal summer conditions — no rope, rack, or anchors needed. Parties who ascended on firm early-season snow should be ready to descend the upper slopes via glissade or a controlled snow descent with an ice axe instead of scree, and should watch for rockfall from parties above given the generally loose rock on this route.
hazards: loose rock on the ridge
long approach
unmaintained/fading trail past the old mine site

waysIn.name: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
waysIn.season: The upper slopes face south and are normally clear from about early July. Earlier in the season, firmer snow makes the loose upper talus easier to travel at the cost of carrying an axe and crampons.
waysIn.notes: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine beside a little tarn on the northeast side of the peak, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
hazards: The mapped trail is abandoned and largely invisible leaving the meadows
Heavy deadfall low down, with long stretches of climbing over and under log jams
No maintained tread and no reliable cairns; the boot path that does exist is short and intermittent
Loose class 2 and 3 boulders and scree on the crest, with route choice left entirely to the party
Water is limited to the stream near the tarn — nothing dependable above it

name: Accendo Lunae (LiB/West Face Var.)
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), take the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain to Colchuck Lake — forest walking along Mountaineer Creek, a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, turning left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, then a final boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Fill water here. Continue around the lake's west shore to its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, exposed to wet-snow slips into July), then break climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Accendo Lunae — a linkup that starts on Let It Burn's line and finishes via a West Face variation — begins at the same point in the base gully as Let It Burn, on the wall's lower-left section, before diverging upward. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the wall; rope up if uncertain.
descent: Because Accendo Lunae finishes by joining a West Face variation, it shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard summit descent: scramble class 3-4 around the right side of the true summit block (bypassing the balanced boulder) to the sandy scree/talus gully, then descend clockwise around the peak back to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr). A short section near the top is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn on the east side (natural anchor) rather than downclimbed. No full rappel of the route line itself is needed.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the formation

name: Accidental Discharge (East Face)
approach: One approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching South Peak. That way arrives on the Chickamin Glacier on the west side of the crest, while this route starts out of the moat of the Blue Glacier on the east side; the approach from the east up Agnes Creek puts you on that side directly. Either way this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
descent: Rappel off the summit by the same line as the peak's other routes: about 35 m north, then a second rappel east onto the Blue Glacier. The last rappel can hang free over the moat at the foot of the face, so land beyond the lip and carry cord to build or back up anchors rather than relying on fixed gear. Do not plan on reversing the loose line of ascent.
hazards: Route features loose, poor quality rock
Contains scary offwidth/chimney sections with sketchy protection

waysIn.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
waysIn.season: July to September, once the bushwhacking is out of snow and the glaciers are travellable.
waysIn.notes: The long way in from the west. Start at the Downey Creek trailhead off the Suiattle River Road and work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor — Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek — on rugged, largely off-trail ground with real bushwhacking and glacier travel. Budget a full day, often two, before you are anywhere near rock. This is an experienced-mountaineers approach and nothing about it is a walk-in.
hazards: Open moat at the foot of the face; the last rappel can hang free over it, so land beyond the lip
Loose, poor-quality rock from the first pitch up; P2 offwidth is bad and sketchy to protect
Glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the approach and directly below the climb
Multi-day, off-trail Ptarmigan corridor approach with heavy bushwhacking and no quick exit
Rockfall on the face; the loose line of ascent should not be reversed
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the west side or linking the climb into a Ptarmigan Traverse trip, accepting a longer, rougher approach than the ferry and Agnes Creek line.

waysIn.name: Agnes Creek from the east
waysIn.notes: The other documented way into this range comes from the east, via the lake ferry and the long trail up Agnes Creek before leaving it for the brush. Parties using it camp on rock ridges above the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing on the same day. It is not a shortcut — the bushwhack off the trail takes most of a day on its own — but it puts you on the glacier side of the crest, which is the side this route starts from.
hazards: Full day of brush off the Agnes Creek trail before any alpine ground
Crevasses and a persistent moat at the foot of the east faces
Loose, poor-quality rock from the first pitch up; P2 offwidth is bad and sketchy to protect
Last rappel can hang free over the moat; land beyond the lip and carry cord for anchors
Four similar summits on one crest, easily confused from below
Remote, committing position with a long retreat

name: Round Mountain Trail (Standard Route)
approach: From Leavenworth, drive US Highway 2 west approximately 17.4-17.7 miles (or from Stevens Pass, drive east about 18 miles) to just past the Nason Creek Rest Area. Turn north (right heading west / left heading east) onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road, Forest Road 6910 -- watch for the turn on a curve with fast highway traffic. Follow FR 6910 (good gravel) for about 4.5 miles, then turn onto spur FR 6910-170 and continue roughly 0.1-0.25 mile to the Round Mountain Trailhead.
descent: From the lookout, retrace the 0.3-mile summit spur down to Nason Ridge Trail #1583, follow the ridge trail back across Ninemile Saddle, and descend Round Mountain Trail #1529 through the burn area and forest to the Round Mountain Trailhead on FR 6910. No technical descent gear is needed; the main concerns are the exposed knife-edge saddle in poor weather/ice and the sustained steep first/last 1.6 miles.
hazards: Exposed narrow ridge crossing at Ninemile Saddle with steep drop-offs on both sides.
Limited/no reliable water sources along the trail.
Avalanche-prone south-facing slopes on the Merritt Lake side of Nason Ridge in spring conditions.
Resident mountain goat population near the summit.

waysIn.name: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
waysIn.season: Roughly July through October once the ridge melts out; the lookout is one of the few in the range still staffed.
waysIn.notes: From the highway just past the rest area, turn north onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road (Forest Road 6910) — the turn is on a curve with fast traffic, so watch for it — and follow good gravel a few miles before turning onto the short spur that ends at the Round Mountain Trailhead. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about a mile and a half through forest and an older burn to its junction with Nason Ridge Trail #1583. Turn left and west and follow the ridge trail, which undulates along the crest for a few miles to the lookout spur.
hazards: The turn off the highway is on a blind curve with fast traffic
The ridge trail narrows to a knife edge with steep rock-filled gullies dropping away on both sides
The crest is exposed to weather with no shelter along it
The lower trail climbs steeply through burn with little shade or water

waysIn.name: Merritt Lake trail from the west
waysIn.notes: A longer way in reaches the same ridge trail from the west via the Merritt Lake trail. It is used mainly for through-hikes or when the Round Mountain side is inaccessible.
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a through-hike of Nason Ridge that starts or ends at Merritt Lake; the lake trail descends about 3.5 miles from the ridge, a much longer trip than the direct climb on the Round Mountain trail.

name: Rampart Ridge Scramble
approach: From the Rachel Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft, end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Rd, Exit 62 from I-90), start on Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first ~2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade, crossing several side streams and cascades (reliable water throughout — no need to carry much from the car). At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses Box/Canyon Creek and hits the notorious 'mile from hell': a heavily rooted, rocky boot-beaten climb that gains roughly 1,300 ft in about a mile, with large step-ups and no switchbacks — this is the crux of the approach fitness-wise, not technically hard but brutal with a full pack. The trail tops out at Rachel Lake (4,700 ft, ~3.5-4 mi from the TH); a use trail/climber's path branches right near the outhouse and skirts the north side of the lake, then switchbacks steeply up rocky tread for about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest (~5,100 ft). At the ridge junction, go left (south) for Rampart Lakes or right for Lila Lake/Alta Mountain — for this route, go right toward Lila Lake. The tread is brushy in places but easy to follow; after about 0.3 mile a cairn marks a fork where the Lila Lake trail continues straight and the unsigned climber's path to Alta branches left. Take the left fork, which starts steep and loose with big steps and no shade, and follow the increasingly exposed climber's path along the ridge crest toward Alta's summit block, negotiating three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, and short sections of real exposure (in one section the path skirts a cliff edge — fall consequences are serious here, and the route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge). A helmet is commonly recommended for the final ridge scramble due to loose rock and exposure. Total one-way distance to the 6,274 ft summit is about 9.5-10 km (matches the 19.3 km round trip) with roughly 3,300 ft of total gain.
descent: This is a scramble, not a technical climb — there is no rappelling on this route (rappels: 0). Descend by reversing the exact ascent line: retrace the ridge crest scramble back over the false summits and down the steep, loose lower ridge to the cairned fork, follow the Lila Lake trail back to the Rampart Ridge junction, drop via the steep half-mile rocky switchbacks to Rachel Lake, then retrace Trail #1313 down through the 'mile from hell' (this section is notably harder on tired knees going down — loose rocky step-downs and roots) and out along Box Canyon Creek to the trailhead. Key descent hazards mirror the approach: the exposed ridge-crest sections near the summit (do not descend this route if the ridge is snow-covered or wet — the exposed traverse becomes significantly more dangerous), loose rock on the steep lower ridge (rockfall risk onto anyone below — descend it one at a time), and the steep, rooted, ankle-turning tread on the 'mile from hell' switchbacks. No natural or fixed anchors are used anywhere on this route; parties should not carry a rope expecting to need it, though a short handline could be improvised on the steep lower ridge for less confident scramblers.
hazards: afternoon thunderstorms

waysIn.name: Rachel Lake, Rampart Ridge, and the cairned Alta turnoff on the Lila Lake trail
waysIn.season: July to October. The route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge
waysIn.notes:
From the Rachel Lake trailhead at 2,800 ft, at the end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Road from I-90 exit 62, take Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first 2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek at a gentle grade with reliable water throughout.

At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses the creek and hits the section known locally as the mile from hell: a heavily rooted, rocky climb gaining roughly 1,300 ft in a mile with big step-ups and no switchbacks. It is the fitness crux of the day, not a technical one.

At Rachel Lake, 4,700 ft, a use trail branches right near the outhouse, skirts the lake's north side, and switchbacks steeply about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest at about 5,100 ft. At the ridge junction go right toward Lila Lake; the left branch leads to Rampart Lakes and is not this route. After about 0.3 mile a cairn marks a fork: Lila Lake is straight ahead, and the climbers' path up Alta's south ridge is the left branch.
hazards: Sustained exposure along the ridge crest, including a section skirting a cliff edge
Three false summits and a class 3 downclimb crux near the top
Loose rock and large step-ups on the initial climbers' path
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long exposed crest
Lingering snow in the approach gully in early season

name: Pilgrimage to Mecca
approach: Backpack in via Andrews Creek or Chewuch River trailheads to Upper Cathedral Lake (see West Route approach). From a camp on the lake's north side (Upper Cathedral Lake), spend about 15 minutes walking around the west side of the lake, then scramble up to the base of the Ka'aba Buttress.
descent: From the top of the route, hike east to gain the saddle area of Amphitheater Mountain, then follow the descent trail/slopes south back down to Upper Cathedral Lake to rejoin the approach.
hazards: Loose blocks reported near the start of some pitches
Afternoon thunderstorms typical of the Pasayten in summer
Route-finding on the descent traverse to the saddle

waysIn.name: Upper Cathedral Lake, round the west side of the water to the Ka'aba Buttress
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Note the wall is north-west facing and stays in shade until around three in the afternoon, so an early start here is a cold one
waysIn.notes:
Get to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by whichever of the long trails suits — this is the same basin used for Cathedral Peak, one to two days in from any trailhead.

The climbing is directly above the water, which is why every published approach time is measured in minutes rather than hours: ten to thirty minutes from camp. If you are camped on the north side of the lake, walk around it on the west side and straight up to the buttress.

Amphitheater's crags rise above the lake on the far side, and the two named buttresses on that wall are visible from your first sight of the water: Ka'aba on the left, Middle Finger on the right.
hazards: A snow moat on the left side of the entry block into early July
The north-side descent gully holding firm snow through July
A north-west aspect that stays cold and shaded until mid-afternoon
Very remote — the nearest trailhead is a multi-day walk

name: West Route
approach: Two common trailheads reach the base: (1) Andrews Creek Trailhead (Trail 504) — from Winthrop, take Hwy 20 to County Road 1213/West Chewuch Road, drive ~6 miles to Forest Road 51, continue ~22 miles to the trailhead at the end of the pavement (3,050 ft). Hike via Andrews Pass and the Boundary Trail to Upper Cathedral Lake (roughly 7 hours for a loaded backpacking pace). (2) Chewuch River Trail/Thirtymile Trailhead — a longer approach (about 20 miles and ~4,900 ft gain to Upper Cathedral Lake), also joining near Cathedral Pass. Most parties backpack in and camp at or near Upper Cathedral Lake (~7,380 ft) before a summit day. From the Chewuch River trail, the Lesamiz Trail climbs to the Boundary Trail just short of Upper Cathedral Lake, a way in used on both a July and a September trip.
descent: From the summit plateau, descend the same scree/grass slopes back into the west basin, then follow the boot path down to the trail and back to Upper Cathedral Lake. Parties combining with Cathedral Peak often traverse between the two via a connecting gully rather than returning all the way to the lake between summits.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the summit slopes
Lingering snow in the access basin/gullies into late June or July
Stream crossings on the approach can be hazardous during high runoff (early season)

waysIn.name: Upper Cathedral Lake and the west-side boot path
waysIn.notes: The whole peak is a backpack with a short walk-up bolted onto the end of it. Nearly every party camps at or near Upper Cathedral Lake, around 7,380 ft, and climbs from there. The lake is reached most directly from the Andrews Creek Trailhead at the end of the pavement on Forest Road 51, going in over Andrews Pass and along the Boundary Trail; the Chewuch River option out of Thirtymile is considerably longer and joins the same ground near Cathedral Pass. Once at the lake nothing about the climb is committing: it is grass, scree and boulder from the trail to the top, with the occasional short step where hands come out. Most parties tag Cathedral Peak the same day, and the two are linked by a connecting gully rather than a return to the lake between them.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes and summit plateau
Snow lingering in the access gullies and upper basin into July
High, cold creek crossings on the approach during runoff
Open, treeless plateau with no shelter from afternoon storms
Long day's walk or more from the nearest road

waysIn.name: Chewuch River trail from Thirtymile
waysIn.notes: Start at the Thirtymile trailhead at the end of the Chewuch road and follow the Chewuch River trail up the valley past the Tungsten Creek junction, then climb to Cathedral Pass and drop to Upper Cathedral Lake. It is longer than the Andrews Creek line but on a steady, well-used trail, and many parties walk in one way and out the other as a loop.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes and summit plateau
Snow lingering in the access gullies and upper basin into July
Stream crossings can be hazardous in high early-season runoff
Open, treeless plateau with no shelter from afternoon storms
Considerably longer walk-in from Thirtymile, far from the road
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want a loop, walking in on this trail and out over Andrews Pass or the reverse; confirm the road to Thirtymile is open first.

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Dosewallips Ranger Station (the road-walk/bike-in described separately covers reaching this point, since the Dosewallips River Road washout has closed vehicle access since 2002), pick up the Dosewallips River Trail and go about 1.4 miles to the signed junction with the West Fork Dosewallips Trail. Turn up the West Fork Trail and follow the river valley through old-growth forest roughly 8 miles to Honeymoon Meadows (3,527 ft) — this is the last reliable flat camping and dependable water before the climb, though the West Fork ford here (and a second crossing near Diamond Meadow lower down) can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain, and the trail has substantial blowdown because NPS maintenance has lagged since the road closure. From Honeymoon Meadows continue up switchbacks about 1.2 more miles to Anderson Pass (4,464 ft), the Dosewallips/Quinault divide and junction with the Enchanted Valley trail — roughly 16 miles and the end of maintained tread. At the pass, leave the trail and follow a climbers' boot path north over talus and heather benches about a mile and 700+ ft of gain to the Anderson Glacier moraine (~5,200 ft), passing a small tarn; this is the customary high camp. From the moraine, ascend along the glacier margin/moraine crest toward Flypaper Pass (6,500 ft), the notch between Mount Anderson to the east and 7,033-ft Echo Rock to the west — historically a steep snow finger, now increasingly bare scree and, late season, exposed ice as the finger has receded, making an ice axe/crampons and careful footing important; do this section in spring or early summer, before it melts out. Anderson's Thumb is the prominent sandstone pinnacle in this Flypaper Pass/Echo Rock vicinity (visible from the Anderson Glacier basin around 5,250 ft); below the pass, bear west under Echo Rock and scramble talus and ledges to its base. No water is reliably available above the Anderson Glacier moraine besides snowmelt, so fill up at camp.
descent: Descend Anderson's Thumb by reversing the ascent line: a single rappel from the summit block back down to the notch/col it rises from. The pinnacle is short (an enjoyable climb on solid sandstone, essentially a one-pitch spire), so a single-strand rappel on a 30m rope or a doubled 60m rope is enough to reach the col; because this is an obscure, lightly-visited objective with no documented fixed hardware, expect a natural anchor — a sling around a horn, block, or chockstone — rather than bolts or chains, so carry cordage/rap rings and be prepared to leave gear or build your own anchor. From the col, downclimb and scramble the talus and ledges back down the snow/scree slope to the Anderson Glacier moraine camp. From there it's a full reversal of the approach: drop to Anderson Pass, follow the West Fork Dosewallips Trail back through Honeymoon Meadows to the Dosewallips Ranger Station, then the road-walk/bike-out. Given the ~38-mile round-trip distance and remote setting, most parties treat this as a multi-day trip and descend only to high camp the day of the climb, hiking out the following day rather than going car-to-car.
hazards: exposed spire climbing on the summit block
loose rock in places, though locally described as 'good sandstone'
Eel Glacier travel on approach (Anderson Glacier itself vanished by ~2011 - that basin is now bare rock/moraine/snowfield, not crevassed ice)
very remote central-Olympics location

waysIn.name: West Fork Dosewallips to Anderson Pass and the moraine
waysIn.notes: A long valley walk with the road ridden or walked first, then the West Fork through Honeymoon Meadows to Anderson Pass. From the pass a climbers' boot path runs north over talus and heather benches about a mile to the tarn camp on the old Anderson Glacier moraine near 5,100 ft. The Thumb is climbed off that camp, almost always as an add-on to a day on the Anderson massif rather than as the reason for the trip.
hazards: Bare scree and exposed ice in the Flypaper Pass chute once the snow finger melts out
Loose talus and ledges below Echo Rock on the way to the col
No fixed anchors on the spire — carry cord and rings and expect to leave gear
Very remote central-Olympics setting with a long, committing walk out
No dependable water above the moraine camp besides snowmelt

name: Southeast Ridge
approach: Start at the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 (roughly 3,650 ft). At about 0.5 mile, bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike/Beverly Creek Trail) — do not miss this junction, as a wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek Trail is a commonly reported mistake. Continue to roughly 3.1 miles and turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek Trail), climbing to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles (roughly 5,900-6,000 ft), which opens up the first real views of Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail. From the pass, descend the well-maintained trail on the far side to the south shore of Ingalls Creek at about 6 miles (roughly 4,200-4,250 ft); ford the creek (wading or a footlog depending on the season/year) to reach flat camping at the Fourth Creek/Ingalls Creek confluence. From camp, leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb generally north into the gentle, heather-and-slab Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side, working up open basin terrain beside the southeast ridge, the crest that rises from this side to the southeast spire. The roped climbing follows that crest, about eight pitches to the southeast spire. Hazards: the Ingalls Creek ford can be a real obstacle in early season or after rain; the basin approach involves loose talus and, in shoulder season, hard snow that may warrant an axe and crampons; this is a long, remote approach (partial day just to reach the base) so plan for a car-camp or bivy.
descent: From the true summit, scramble back east along the summit ridge to the top of the South Gully. Its one technical step is a short, blocky rock cleft capped by a chockstone, with a fixed sling above it: rappel it or downclimb it on belay. Below that, descend the long gully and the brushy, forested slope beneath it toward Ingalls Creek, return to camp, and reverse the approach over Fourth Creek Pass to the trailhead. The descent is long, so leave the summit with a comfortable margin of daylight.
hazards: loose rock on the towers
complex route-finding on the crest
afternoon thunderstorms
the long approach and tiring exit
fording Ingalls Creek, which can be difficult and cold in early-season high water

waysIn.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
waysIn.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up beside the southeast ridge. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is outside the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.
hazards: Wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek trail near the start costs much of the day
Ingalls Creek ford is a real obstacle in early season or after rain
Long, remote approach over Fourth Creek Pass; plan a camp or bivy
Teanaway-side trails under a post-fire closure order; confirm status first
Loose rock on the towers and lichen-covered, hard-to-protect blocks on the lower pitches
Route-finding on the crest between the SE spire false summit and the true summit
Afternoon thunderstorms; long tiring exit

waysIn.name: Esmeralda over Longs Pass into Ingalls Creek
waysIn.notes: From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, take the trail to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and drop roughly 1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek. Then follow the Ingalls Creek trail east, downstream, to the camps below Argonaut's south side and climb from there.
hazards: Ingalls Creek valley is brushy, with brush between the trail and open slopes the real work of the approach
Long trail out over Longs Pass with no water on the climb over the pass
Ingalls Creek ford is difficult and cold in early-season high water
Loose rock on the towers and lichen-covered, hard-to-protect blocks on the lower pitches
Route-finding on the crest between the SE spire false summit and the true summit
Afternoon thunderstorms; long tiring exit
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties starting from the Teanaway road end who prefer the views; it climbs more than the Ingalls Creek valley walk, crosses Longs Pass and drops about 1,400 feet to the creek.

name: Around the Cave We Go
approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR 20 near Washington Pass, hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climbers' path that breaks off just past a small stream and climbs slabs, talus and heather to the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. The gully holds snow into early summer, so an ice axe helps early in the season, and rockfall is a concern once it melts out. From the notch, drop about 50 feet down the gully on the north side of the tower to the two diagonal cracks that start the Cave Route. This variation begins at the top of that route's first pitch, so the base of the climb is the same.
descent: This variation leaves the Cave Route at the top of its first pitch and rejoins it, so the descent is the Cave Route's: rappel from the west side of the summit. The usual rappel there takes two ropes, but they can jam on the pull, and a mid-height station lets parties make it with one rope. The rappel lands on a ledge. Move climber's right to a second rappel that follows the first pitch of the North Face down to the saddle shared with Liberty Bell. From the notch, reverse the approach down the gully and through the bowl to the Blue Lake Trail.
hazards: Shared approach gully is loose and prone to rockfall from parties above.

name: South Ridge / Southwest Gully
approach: From the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (River Bend Campground, ~2,700 ft, at the end of Lost River Road/FR 5400), follow the West Fork Methow River Trail roughly 8 miles up-valley to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) at Brush Creek. Turn left (south/west) on the PCT and follow it about 1.5-2 miles, crossing Jet Creek, to Horse Heaven Camp (~4,350 ft) — the last reliable, easy water before the climb (treat before drinking; flows can drop significantly by late season). From camp, pick up the old, unsigned Azurite Pass (Mill Creek) trail, which departs the PCT roughly 120 yards east of the Jet Creek crossing at a small rock cairn — easy to miss, and parties note the tread is faint/braided enough that a GPS track is genuinely useful here. The path switchbacks up through slide-alder brush, firms up into a real trail around 5,000 ft, re-crosses Jet Creek at about 5,300 ft (a rock-hop ford, can run high with snowmelt in June/early July), then climbs through eroded, brushy benches before breaking out into open heather meadows and granite slabs just below Azurite Pass (6,700 ft) — roughly 3-3.5 hours from Horse Heaven Camp. From the pass, leave the trail and work northeast/east up a mix of krummholz, sand, scree, and talus to a broad shoulder around 7,400 ft, then follow a gently rising traverse, marked with ducks and cairns, over a succession of ribs, gullies, and sandy slopes toward the base of the summit tower. The final push climbs a prominent south/southwest-facing gully — loose underfoot (watch for rockfall onto party members below) but no harder than Class 3 in dry conditions; it can hold firm snow well into summer, in which case an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is on the order of 12-13 miles with about 6,700 ft of gain, so most parties backpack in to Horse Heaven Camp and climb from there rather than doing it car-to-car.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the summit gully to the 7,400-ft shoulder, back across the ducked/cairned rib-and-gully traverse to Azurite Pass, and down the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass climbers' trail to Horse Heaven Camp and the PCT/West Fork Methow Trail back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb for the majority of parties in normal summer, dry-rock conditions — no fixed rappel stations exist on the route. The one exception is the summit gully itself: in early season or after a fresh snowfall, the gully can hold firm, steep snow or verglas that makes downclimbing dicey, and parties in that situation have set up a single rappel through the gully on natural anchors (boulders/chockstones/slung horns — there is no fixed gear) rather than downclimb. A 30 m rope is reported to be not long enough to get through the gully in one rappel, so bring a 60 m rope (doubled, i.e. effectively a ~30 m rappel) or plan on two shorter rappels/a lower-out if snow conditions demand it. Loose rock in the gully is a hazard on both the climb and any rappel — helmets on, and be mindful of rope-dislodged debris hitting the second or trailing party. Outside of that scenario, treat the descent as class 2-3 talus/scree hiking requiring careful route-finding to stay on the ducked line back to the pass.
hazards: routefinding on upper slopes
afternoon thunderstorms

waysIn.name: Azurite Pass, the 7,400 ft shoulder and the west-face traverse
waysIn.notes: From Azurite Pass leave the trail and work northeast and east up krummholz, sand, scree and talus to a flat shoulder at about 7,400 ft — flat enough that parties cache overnight gear on it, and easy to relocate on the way down. Continue up the crest to roughly 7,600 ft, where a lower south summit obstructs the ridge and the well-cairned climbers' route drops off westward. From there a gently rising traverse, clearly marked by ducks and cairns, crosses a succession of ribs, gullies and sandy slopes, staying below the cliffs rather than in them, and crossing two or three short snow runnels that an ice axe handles. The traverse runs toward the peak's prominent west rib.
hazards: Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully; stay out of each other's fall line
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Two or three short snow runnels to cross on the west-face traverse
Many similar ribs and gullies; turning up too late puts you on the southwest face
Exposed class 3 on the traverse and summit gully
Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open upper ridge

waysIn.name: Harts Pass and the Pacific Crest Trail south
waysIn.notes: Start high at Harts Pass and follow the Pacific Crest Trail south to Horse Heaven Camp, where the old Mill Creek trail climbs to Azurite Pass. It avoids the lower West Fork Methow trail, which has been brushy and slow past its first few miles.
hazards: Long approach on the Pacific Crest Trail with a sustained climb to Azurite Pass
Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Exposed class 3 on the west-face traverse and summit gully
Route-finding among ribs and gullies on the upper slopes
Afternoon thunderstorm exposure on the open upper ridge
waysIn.whyThisWay: To skip the brushy, slow lower West Fork Methow trail by starting high at Harts Pass and walking the crest trail south to Horse Heaven.

waysIn.name: Canyon Creek and Mill Creek from SR-20
waysIn.notes: From the Canyon Creek trailhead on SR-20, follow Canyon Creek to the Mill Creek trail and up past the old Azurite Mine to the west slopes of the peak or on to Azurite Pass. The Mill Creek trail is badly overgrown in places and route-finding through alder is slow, so most parties prefer the east-side starts.
hazards: Mill Creek trail badly overgrown, with slow alder route-finding
Long approach; Azurite Pass under snow into July in a normal year
Loose, disintegrating rock on the traverse and in the final gully
Final gully often holds steep snow into midsummer; axe, crampons if icy
Exposed class 3 on the west-face traverse and summit gully
Afternoon thunderstorms; no shelter near the pass
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want to start straight from the highway and can put up with an overgrown Mill Creek trail and slow alder route-finding.

name: Diobsud Creek Glacier
approach: Drive Baker Lake Road (FR-11) to FR-1106, then FR-1107 to its end at the Watson Lakes Trailhead (~4,360 ft, Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness boundary nearby). Start on the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail (Trail #611), which climbs gently through forest for about 1 mile to a junction with the Anderson Butte Trail (#611.1); stay left/straight on #611. Continue about another half mile to a second junction, about 1.5 miles from the trailhead — the right fork drops 0.5 mile to Lower Anderson Lake, while the climber's route bears left and climbs to a ridge saddle (~600 ft above the trailhead) where the trail crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping toward the Watson Lakes. From this saddle, leave the maintained tread and pick up a boot path heading south along the ridge, staying high above Lower Anderson Lake, through meadows to Upper Anderson Lake (~5,100-5,300 ft) — the last easy, reliable water before things get rougher. From Upper Anderson Lake, angle northeast up a short wooded gully, then continue across open rock slabs, scree, and lingering snowfields on Mt. Watson's north side, crossing another saddle near 5,300 ft before descending through heather to the Diobsud Lakes basin (figure roughly 5-6 hours car-to-lakes for a fit party) — the last dependable camp/water source below the peak. From Diobsud Lakes the route turns unpleasant: sidehilling across slippery vegetation, brush and cedar thickets, mossy slab scrambling, and steep dirt/scree gullies with real loose-rock hazard lead up onto Bacon's south ridge. Once on the south ridge, broad snow slopes lead onto the toe of the Diobsud Creek Glacier. Rope up here — the glacier holds real crevasse hazard (parties report needing to probe, especially early and late season, though the upper apron is sometimes reported clean in a good snow year) — and climb/traverse northwest toward the col below the summit pyramid (roughly 6,200-6,300 ft), finishing on broad summit snow slopes to a short summit arête. Snow condition (firm morning snow vs. slushy afternoon) matters a lot on both the gully and glacier sections, so an early start is standard. The gully leading from Diobsud Lakes basin up to the south ridge/glacier access can be avalanche-prone in snow-covered conditions.
descent: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: down the summit snow slopes and col, back onto and down the Diobsud Creek Glacier (roped, same crevasse caution as the approach), down through the steep loose gully/south-ridge terrain to Diobsud Lakes, then back over the Mt. Watson sidehill, saddle, and Anderson Lakes ridge path to the Watson Lakes Trailhead. This is a walk-off/glacier-descent — no rappels are used on the standard round trip; the technical difficulty is glacier travel and loose, steep downclimbing rather than anything requiring rope-anchored lowering. Parties continuing north as part of a longer Bacon-Hagan-Blum (or Watson-Bacon-Hagan-Blum) traverse instead descend from the summit down quick snow slopes to the "Bacon Tarns" (small meltwater ponds sitting on a rock bench beneath the Green Lake Glacier), then follow heather and meadow along Bacon's north ridge, passing high above Green Lake toward Hidden Lake, continuing the traverse rather than returning to the Watson Lakes trailhead. Either way, expect the same loose-rock and brush hazards on the south-ridge gully in reverse, and re-assess glacier conditions/crevasse bridges on the return trip since afternoon snow softening changes the picture from the morning ascent.
hazards: glacier travel and crevasse risk
long, arduous bushwhack approach
afternoon thunderstorms
steep, avalanche-prone gully accessing the glacier

waysIn.name: Anderson Lakes and the saddle chain to the northeast camp
waysIn.notes: Take the Watson Lakes Trail from the road end and, at the saddle beyond the Lower Anderson Lake fork, leave the maintained tread for a hiker's path heading south along the ridge, well above Lower Anderson Lake. The path then opens out into meadows and reaches Upper Anderson Lake — the last easy water. From the lake, go northeast up a short wooded gully and carry on in that direction onto open moraine and heather slopes around 5,300 ft. Pass beneath the Watson peaks, descending to about 5,000 ft to skirt a buttress on their east side; climb next to a saddle at 5,360 ft and cross over to the south side of the ridge. Then head east, dropping a little toward the next low point of the ridge, a saddle near 4,900 ft, and cross a short buttress on easy ledges along the way. A good camp sits at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of Bacon Peak.
hazards: No tread, no signage and no marked line above Upper Anderson Lake
Lingering snowfields on the traverse beneath the Watson peaks
Crevasse hazard on the icecap if the line drifts onto it
Featureless snow slopes near the top — navigation in whiteout is the real difficulty

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the pullout along FR 6835 (West Fork Foss Road) — just past the concrete bridge over the East Fork Foss River, about half a mile from its junction with FR 68 and roughly 5.2 miles from US-2 at Skykomish — there is no maintained trail. Climbers cross to the north side of the road and pick up the toe of Bald Eagle's north ridge at about 1,600 ft, entering second-growth forest thick with fallen timber that requires weaving/scrambling over deadfall for the first few hundred feet of gain. Stay on or near the ridge crest heading south-southeast; around 2,600 ft the forest transitions to older growth and the underbrush thins out, making travel noticeably easier and the ridgeline easy to follow with few reasons to leave it. The going stays moderate until roughly 4,500 ft, where the ridge narrows and steepens into the trip's brushiest stretch — a pointier crest with real drop-offs on both sides, dense small trees/slide alder crowding the tread, and (in season) heavy mosquito pressure; move carefully here as exposure picks up. By 5,200 ft the ridge opens into rockier, more open terrain, with snow patches lingering later into the season (more persistent on the east side of the crest than on the drier, rockier ridge itself). At about 5,400 ft the ridge runs into a cliff band directly below the summit — this is the route's crux: bypass it by veering left (east) off the crest into a small gully and taking a rising traverse into the upper summit basin rather than attempting the band head-on. The final approach to the 6,259 ft summit crosses steep snow and a few small trees for the last ~20 vertical feet; helmet is warranted here for rockfall off the cliff band, and in early-to-mid season an ice axe and light traction (microspikes/crampons) are worth carrying for the final snow pitch and for the traverse below 5,400 ft. There is no reliable water source directly on the ridge once you leave the East Fork Foss River at the trailhead, so carry what you need. Best conditions are July–September; the route is class 3-4 scrambling with no roped climbing required on a dry ridge.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — descend by reversing the North Ridge exactly as ascended; there is no rappelling on the standard route. From the summit, downclimb the steep snow/small-tree section back to the top of the 5,400 ft cliff band, then carefully reverse the rising traverse and gully bypass on the east side of the crest to regain the ridge crest below the cliffs — this bypass is the one spot demanding real route-finding and careful downclimbing (loose rock and exposure in the gully), so many parties down-face here rather than walk it. Below 5,200 ft, follow the open rocky ridge back into the brushy, exposed 4,500-5,200 ft stretch, staying on the crest to avoid the steep drop-offs to either side. Once back into old-growth forest below 4,500 ft the ridge broadens and travel gets easy and fast; one party found the descent takes well under half the time of the ascent once past the brush and cliff band. Continue down through the second-growth/deadfall lower forest to regain FR 6835 at the East Fork Foss River bridge pullout. No technical anchors (bolted or natural) are used on this route — it is entirely natural terrain.
hazards: off-trail routefinding
steep brushy, exposed terrain with drop-offs
lingering snow and ice on north-facing slopes into summer
afternoon thunderstorms

waysIn.name: North ridge direct from the Foss River Road bridge
waysIn.notes: There is no trail of any kind. Park on the road shoulder just past the concrete bridge over the East Fork Foss River, cross to the far side of the road, and go straight into the forest to pick up the toe of the north ridge around 1,600 ft. The first several hundred feet of gain are spent weaving over down timber rather than walking; near 2,600 ft the forest turns to older growth and the underbrush thins so the crest becomes easy to follow. Moderate going holds until about 4,500 ft, where the ridge narrows and steepens into the brushiest stretch of the day, then opens into rock and heather by 5,200 ft. Carry all your water from the river — nothing above the road is dependable.
hazards: No trail and no marked start from the road
Down timber low down, then slide alder and small trees crowding a narrow crest between 4,500 and 5,200 ft
Hard snow and ice in the bypass gully and on the traverse into midsummer
Rockfall off the cliff band above the traverse
No water anywhere above the river

name: Standard Route
approach: The climber/hiker trailhead is at the end of FR 2870 (signed Baldy/Tyler Peak trailhead, ~12-car gravel pullout, roughly 47.883, -123.143) in the Upper Dungeness drainage of the Hood Canal Ranger District. From the trailhead, follow the old roadbed a short distance; at about 0.3 mile the Baldy climber's path (Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816) splits off to the right and begins climbing in earnest. At roughly 0.5 mile (~3,600 ft) the trail crosses a decommissioned logging road. Mueller Creek parallels the route through these early switchbacks and is the last reliable water low on the mountain — top off here, especially in late summer. The only water higher up is a small meadow stream reached by a short, steep side path just below where the trail gains the ridge crest, and nothing flows above that. Around 1.3 miles the path crosses the old Maynard Burn track near a brief junction with the Upper Dungeness Trail (#833.2) before continuing up as the Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816.2). Hikers describe this middle section as a relentless, eroded 'staircase' — expect a narrow tread (in spots barely a foot wide) sidehilling an eroding slope, crumbly footing crossing a rocky ravine, and faint, muddy tread through boggy meadow benches where flagging/cairns can be sparse. By about 2 miles the forest thins and Tyler Peak comes into view; by 2.7 miles (~6,200 ft) the trail gains the open ridge crest/saddle east of Baldy, with the first views north to the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Vancouver Island — this is also where the route leaves the trees for good, an important landmark for the return. From the saddle, a boot path continues west along the exposed ridge, over a false summit (roughly 6,500 ft, frequently mistaken for the true top and a common confusion point in poor visibility) to the actual summit at 3.6 miles / 6,808 ft, which has an old campsite. Total is about 7.2 miles and 3,800 ft round trip. The ridge is fully exposed to wind and cloud, and lingering snow can bury the boot path into June; carry a map/GPS track for the upper mountain.
descent: Descend the same Standard Route (out-and-back), and no rappelling is required (0 rappels) — this is a hike/scramble, not a technical rock route. The main descent hazard is route-finding: the boot path across the open ridge and meadow benches above ~6,200 ft is faint and easily lost in the fog/whiteout conditions that frequently roll in on this exposed summit, and several trip reports specifically describe hikers becoming disoriented near the false summit on the way down. Note landmarks on the way up — the false summit at roughly 6,500 ft, and the point at 2.7 miles/~6,200 ft where the trail first exits treeline onto the ridge — as handrails for the descent, and carry a GPS track of the ascent line if visibility is questionable. Once back below ~5,400 ft the route re-enters forest and the tread becomes obvious again, following the Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816.2) down through the Lower Maynard Burn Trail (#816) switchbacks, crossing the old decommissioned road and Mueller Creek drainage, back to the FR 2870 trailhead.
hazards: Steep, eroded, narrow tread with real exposure on the switchbacking staircase section below ~5,400 ft
Lingering snow patches on the upper open ridge and false summit into late June in some years — ice axe/traction may be warranted
Loose, exposed scree with rockfall risk on the ridge beyond Baldy toward Gray Wolf Ridge; parties there typically spread out and wear helmets
Wind- and lightning-exposed, treeless summit and ridge — afternoon storm exposure with no cover
Unmaintained boot path above 5,400 ft can be hard to follow in fog/low visibility

waysIn.name: Maynard Burn climbers' path from the Dungeness
waysIn.notes: From the gravel pullout at the end of the forest road, follow the old roadbed a short way; at about a third of a mile the climbers' path splits right and starts climbing in earnest. Mueller Creek in the first switchbacks is the last dependable water low on the mountain; the only water higher is a small stream down a steep side path near the ridge crest. The middle section is a narrow, eroded staircase — tread barely a foot wide in places, sidehilling an eroding slope, with crumbly footing across a rocky ravine and faint muddy going through boggy meadow benches.
hazards: Narrow, eroded tread with genuine exposure below about 5,400 ft
Snow lingering on the open upper ridge into late June
Treeless, wind- and lightning-exposed crest with no shelter
Faint boot path across the meadow benches, easily lost in fog
Loose scree and rockfall on the continuation toward Gray Wolf Ridge

name: North Face
approach: Park at the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,280 ft, end of gravel Forest Road 6024/Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near the town of Baring); a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the self-issue kiosk. This is the same trailhead used for the Barclay Lake day-hike and for Baring's easier South/West Ridge route, but for the North Face, leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts behind the outhouse rather than on the main trail. Follow an old, abandoned logging road for about 1/3 mile to a cairn (~2,450 ft) where a rough, unmaintained climbers' path splits off toward the base of the mountain — this is easy to miss and is not marked by any trail sign. From the cairn, the boot path climbs steep, loose dirt slopes and crosses the creek draining the face several times; stay close to the water to keep the correct line, since the tread is faint and frequently lost in the brush. At roughly 4,300 ft — about 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — the path reaches Couloir Camp, the historic base camp used during the decade-long siege that produced the first ascent; it remains a reasonable first-night bivy for parties who want to break the approach into two shorter days. Above Couloir Camp, the route continues up between two precipitous, brush-and-cliff-covered rock ribs that flank a large couloir (snow often lingers here into August, so early-season parties may want an axe for this section) to reach the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead. In total, the lower approach involves fighting through approximately 2,300 vertical feet of dense brush (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club) and forest before any technical rock climbing begins — expect around 7 hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear sturdy approach shoes or boots rather than carrying rock shoes for this section.
descent: Do not plan to reverse the technical wall — virtually every account of climbing Baring's north face describes descending a separate walk-off line rather than rappelling the route from top to bottom. From the top of the wall, traverse west/climber's-left (some parties describe following an old 'base-jumper' boot path) around to a talus field and the notch between Baring's summits, then drop roughly 700 vertical feet through boulders and meadow to pick up a heather trail on skier's left. This connects to a game trail switchbacking down through old-growth forest, a roughly one-mile traverse along the ridgecrest, and then a steep switchbacking trail (~1,500 vertical ft) down to a clearing and old logging road that returns to the Barclay Lake Trailhead — about 3 hours car-to-summit-to-car for the descent leg on the routes this has been documented for. This walk-off is a scramble/hike, not a rappel descent, and no fixed rappel stations are established on it. That said, treat this as route- and finish-dependent: Baring's north face has multiple independent lines topping out at different points, some of which may not connect cleanly to the walk-off gully without downclimbing or short rope work, and the 1961 first-ascent party made long rappels down the upper walls to retreat/descend in fog when the walk-off wasn't known or reachable. If you retreat mid-route, or finish on a line that doesn't top out near the notch, be prepared to rappel — carry a 60m rope and rack for building anchors, since fixed/bolted rappel stations should not be assumed on this poorly-protected, historically loose-rock alpine wall; natural anchors (trees, horns, gear) are the norm. Given this uncertainty, treat rappel count as route-specific and unknown rather than fixed.
hazards: serious routefinding
long committing face
retreat difficult

waysIn.name: Barclay Lake trailhead to Couloir Camp and the North Face
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep; snow lingers in the couloir into August
waysIn.notes:
Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near Baring; Northwest Forest Pass at the self-issue kiosk.

Leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts behind the outhouse, not on the main trail. Follow the old abandoned logging road about a third of a mile to a cairn at roughly 2,450 ft where a rough unmaintained path splits off toward the base of the mountain. That split is easy to miss and carries no trail sign.

From the cairn the boot path climbs steep loose dirt and crosses the creek draining the face several times. Stay close to the water: the tread is faint and repeatedly lost in the brush, and the creek is the handrail. In total the lower approach fights through roughly 2,300 vertical feet of dense slide alder, vine maple and devil's club before any technical rock. Allow around seven hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear boots or sturdy approach shoes rather than carrying them.
hazards: Missing the unsigned cairn split at ~2,450 ft
About 2,300 ft of slide alder, vine maple and devil's club
Faint tread constantly lost in brush — losing the creek loses the line
Steep loose dirt slopes
Snow in the couloir between the ribs into August

name: North Buttress
approach: From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (~3,100 ft, end of Ruth Creek Rd/FR-32) follow Hannegan Pass Trail #674 — nearly level for the first mile, then a steady grade — about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Hannegan Pass (5,100 ft), roughly 2.5-3 hours. Drop off the back (east) side of the pass and continue about 5 more miles, bearing right at the North Cascades National Park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper; this section loses elevation into the valley, passes U.S. Cabin backcountry camp, and reaches the Chilliwack River crossing (historically a hand-cable car — verify current status with the NPS, since a high-water ford here is a real hazard). Continue down-valley past Copper Creek/Brush Creek camps to the Bear Creek confluence, roughly 17 miles and 8-9 hours from the trailhead including the pass. At Bear Creek, leave the maintained trail: ford Bear Creek (can be a genuine, sketchy crossing during snowmelt) and climb steep, brushy timber eastward. Above treeline the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake; from there traverse the divide, skirting the south slopes of Points 6592 and 6822 and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft — the standard high camp, with running water and heather tent sites. All told this is roughly 21 miles and about 6,500 ft of gain from the trailhead to camp, which most parties split over two days, camping on the Chilliwack River Trail near Brush Creek because the Bear Creek camp has been closed since the 2021 fire. A much shorter line (~9 miles to camp) starts from Chilliwack Lake Road in BC, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry and follows an overgrown, unmaintained tread after the first 1.7 miles; the Hannegan approach is the one to plan on. From high camp, the route itself begins with a descent: drop down steep scree trending climbers' right off the saddle, cross several minor gullies, and reach the toe of the small glacier/névé spilling from the couloir below the North Buttress (about 60-90 minutes); crampons and an axe are genuinely useful here even in summer. Climb the glacier/névé on the climber's-left side of the buttress and work into slabs leading to the corner system that marks the start of the technical climbing, staying alert for a moat where the névé meets rock.
descent: The standard descent off Bear Mountain's summit is a walk-off, not a rappel-mandatory line: traverse west/southwest staying on the south side of the summit crest, cross a notch/gap, and work across a snowfield that breaks the cliff bands above the Bear Creek drainage, then continue down easier 3rd-4th class terrain. A short, sometimes-loose 3rd class gully drops back down to the saddle camp at ~6,480 ft — about 1 hour and 1,400-1,500 ft of descent in good conditions. That said, this gully is exposed enough that a meaningful number of parties choose to back it up rather than down-climb it, especially with wet rock, a less-experienced partner, or an alpine-start-to-dusk timeline: a party that prefers not to downclimb it can rappel off natural anchors, though no rappel is required. There are no fixed bolted anchors on this remote, lightly-trafficked route — build natural anchors (horns, gear placements, slung blocks) and back up any old tat you find in place before weighting it. Below the gully, reverse the approach: regain the saddle, traverse back past Points 6822/6592 into the meadows above Ruta Lake, descend through brush and timber to re-ford Bear Creek, and rejoin the Chilliwack River Trail for the long hike back over Hannegan Pass to the trailhead.
hazards: very remote committing position
loose rock on sections
long approach and descent
sustained exposure

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
waysIn.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
waysIn.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
hazards: Chilliwack River crossing depends on a cable car being in service; serious ford if not
Bear Creek ford in snowmelt can be committing
Steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread above Bear Creek
Loose south-facing slopes on the divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the shrinking glacier in the couloir
Moat between neve and slab worsens through the season
Days from any road; loose, hard-to-protect rock on the buttress

waysIn.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
waysIn.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
waysIn.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and this page cannot say that crossing is lawful, so confirm it with the border authorities before planning on it; and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
hazards: Border crossing on foot with no port of entry; legality unconfirmed
Unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
Loose south-facing slopes on the divide traverse
Rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant beneath the buttress
Loose, hard-to-protect rock on the buttress
Remote position; a rescue may involve two countries
waysIn.whyThisWay: Normally the shortest way in, but it crosses into the United States on foot away from a port of entry, which is not permitted.

name: Church Lake Scramble
approach: From the FS 3160 road-end parking (roughly 48.957°N, 121.851°W, reached via Canyon Creek Road/FS 31 then FS 3160 as noted above), the route follows an unmaintained but well-worn boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail, just a heavily used user track — that climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft of gain to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake sitting in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first pitch is the steepest sustained grade of the day. Skirt the lake along its east/left shore (best flat campsites are on the far side, useful if splitting the trip). Beyond the lake the trail fades into intermittent boot-path and cairns through meadows and heather benches; keep left (east) up the basin rim toward a broad knoll around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block — this stretch accounts for most of the remaining ~900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 mi one-way (matching the ~5.9 km round trip). From the 6,066 ft knoll, drop slightly and traverse north across a rocky/heather bowl toward the base of Bearpaw's summit block; the final approximately 300 ft to the 6,091 ft summit is easy class 2-3 scrambling on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure in the last pitch. Church Lake is the last reliable water source — carry water from there for the upper mountain. There is no maintained tread past the lake, so route-finding by cairns and boot-path is necessary, and in early/mid-season lingering snow on the steep initial slope above the lake and in the summit gullies can require an ice axe and caution; parties often find snow patches into July on shaded sections. In July the last four miles of the Forest Service road to the trailhead are steep and deeply rutted; a high-clearance all-wheel-drive or 4x4 vehicle is the safe choice, and a phone map may send you to a different trailhead, so aim for the road end.
descent: Descend the same line: from the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 scramble terrain back to the 6,066 ft knoll above Church Lake basin. From there most parties either retrace the rim/boot-path back down into the basin, or drop via a direct scree/dirt gully (chute) that cuts straight down from the ridge to the lake's shore, shortcutting the traverse — this chute is loose underfoot (scree and dirt over rock) and warrants care with footing and any parties below; if snow lingers in the chute (common into early summer) an ice axe and basic self-arrest awareness are worthwhile. From Church Lake, retrace the 0.6-0.7 mile boot path back down to the FS 3160 trailhead. This is a non-technical walk-off/downclimb scramble — no rope or rappelling is used on this route.
hazards: exposed class 3 ridge near the summit
heather and slab when wet

Intermittent cairns through meadows and heather with nothing built to follow

Church Lake is the last water

name: Beckey-Tate
approach: From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20, follow the cairned climbers' trail south along the west side of Early Winters Creek toward Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak, but stay on the trail (right/west side of the creek) longer than the Southwest Rib/West Face line does — do not cross the creek where that route splits off. Continue up-valley as the trail fades into open talus and boulder fields, then work toward the head of the basin, cutting left (east) toward the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon. This drops/traverses you into the south-facing basin directly below Big Kangaroo's south wall, where the Beckey-Tate's obvious central ramp-and-ledge system is visible splitting the face. The approach is noticeably longer and more sustained than the standard West Face gully route — expect talus hopping and some brush, roughly 2 miles and 2,440 ft one-way to the base (with the full route running to about 3,166 ft of gain at the 8,326 ft summit), with 2.5-5 hours a reasonable estimate given the routefinding through boulder fields. Early-season parties will likely find snow lingering in the approach basin and in the gullies near the top of the route, so a light axe and crampons are worth carrying into early-mid summer.
descent: Do not plan to rappel the Beckey-Tate line itself — while it's technically possible with two ropes (roughly five or six rappels off slings and trees), the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, making rope-stuck and rockfall risk high; most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead, from the top of the route scramble about 20 ft up and left to reach the notch that separates the south face from the true summit, which stands a few hundred feet higher. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches to the unprotected 5.6 summit slab (protected by a single old bolt), which is downclimbed or top-roped; then descend the shared gully: two slung-block anchors get you down with one or two single-rope rappels (a 60m rope is sufficient either way) through the steep/loose upper gully, after which it's a scree-and-snow walk/glissade down the gully back to the approach basin, across Early Winters Creek, and out the climbers' trail to the Hairpin Turn. Expect the full descent to take a couple of hours; keep helmets on throughout given the loose rock in the gully.
hazards: loose rock
runout chimney pitches with sparse protection
early-season snow/ice on the approach and descent gullies

waysIn.name: The Hairpin turnout, staying west of the creek longer than the West Face line, then over the Half Moon col into the south basin
waysIn.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20, follow the cairned climbers' trail south along the west side of Early Winters Creek toward Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, but stay on the trail, on the right or west side of the creek, longer than the west face line does. Do not cross the creek where that route splits off.

Continue up-valley as the trail fades into open talus and boulder fields, then work toward the head of the basin. Roughly 2 miles and 2,440 ft one-way to the base, with 2.5-5 hours a reasonable estimate given the route-finding through boulder fields. Noticeably longer and more sustained than the standard West Face gully route.
hazards: Talus hopping and route-finding through boulder fields for 2 miles
A lot of large loose rock on the route, making rappelling it inadvisable
An exposed unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old bolt if tagging the true summit
A steep, loose upper gully on the shared descent
Snow lingering in the approach basin and the gullies near the top of the route in early season

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the FR 4096 spur (reached via Mountain Loop Highway to just past Bedal Campground, then up FR 4096), the actual hike starts at an unsigned, unmaintained climber's boot path around 2,100–2,200 ft, roughly 1.3 miles up the spur road near its second or third switchback. The trailhead is marked only by a small cairn/rock pile in the roadside grass and is notoriously easy to drive past — worth GPS-marking on the way in. The path drops into forest and follows Merry Brook (also called Merry Creek) upstream — the last reliable water on route — before swinging north out of the drainage to gain a forested ridge around 2,600 ft. Expect a genuinely unmaintained track with blowdown, brush, and a few faint braids; pink flagging tied roughly every 100 yards helps confirm you're on line, but parties still regularly lose the path, so download a GPS track before you go. Above the ridge the trail climbs through a first boulder field around 3,500 ft (moss-covered talus, easiest when snow-free), passes above a small tarn (Nels Lake) with a cascade audible below, then reaches a second boulder field near 4,200 ft that often holds snow into summer, with views opening north to Spring Mountain around 4,300 ft. By roughly 4,450 ft the route is typically on solid snow in early/mid-season. The technical crux comes around 4,900–5,200 ft at a cliff band below the summit massif: parties look for a ramp/notch line rather than the more direct gully (a moat-like gap has been found there and is best avoided), and the rock is mossy and loose in spots, occasionally icy where snow meets rock — a short hand-line is sometimes used here by less experienced climbers. A short descending traverse east through overgrown brush and devil's club near 5,200 ft regains the ridge above treeline, after which it's a straightforward snow climb and crossing of low-angle granite slabs to the east ridge — an easy, minimally-exposed Class 2–3 scramble toward the summit.
descent: Descent reverses the ascent (Merry Brook) line — there is no separate down-route. Parties often find the descent harder than the climb: downclimbing the exposed summit slab traverse and the mossy/icy cliff-band crux takes real care, with at least one party specifically noting they wished for a helmet on the exposed section between holds. In the boulder fields, downclimbing large talus is markedly slower and more awkward than ascending it. Early-season (roughly through June) parties can often glissade or plunge-step the snow gullies below the cliff band and on the upper slopes, cutting real time off the descent; by August most of this has melted out to loose talus, heather, and bare rock, so plan on a slower boot descent and watch closely for the pink flagging, since it's easy to drift off-route in the boulder fields and brush, especially in fading light. This is a downclimb, not a rappel route: the cliff-band crux and the summit slab crux are both downclimbed by the large majority of parties. A rope, a sling rigged as a hasty hand-line, or a couple of pieces are occasionally carried for these two crux moves by less experienced or more cautious parties — especially if the rock is wet or the snow/rock interface is icy — but this is a self-belay/hand-line setup, not a rappel, and no fixed or natural rappel anchors are established anywhere on the route. Budget real time: car-to-car days typically run roughly 9–12 hours (one June party took about 10 hours, and a Mountaineers club outing took roughly 9 hours).
hazards: notorious brushy, route-finding-intensive approach through old-growth forest and devil's club
crux cliff band at roughly 4,900-5,100 ft: mossy/duff-covered rock, often icy into early summer, described by trip reports as the most dangerous part of the route
loose Class 3 rock and 'veggie belay' (unreliable brush holds) on the upper mountain
steep heather and snow gullies that cliff out if followed too far (stay right of the direct gully near the crux)
afternoon thunderstorms common in summer over the Mountain Loop corridor
wet-slide/wet-slab avalanche potential on the north-facing snowfields above the cliff band in spring

waysIn.name: Merry Brook path and the key ramp
waysIn.notes: Start from the unsigned boot path off the FR 4096 spur, marked only by a small cairn and rock pile in the roadside grass and notoriously easy to drive past — accounts disagree on the mileage and on which switchback it leaves from, so mark it on the way in rather than trusting a figure. The path drops into forest and follows Merry Brook upstream, the last reliable water, then swings north out of the drainage onto a forested ridge. It is aggressively steep with deadfall to climb under and over, and eases where it turns south above and just west of a small tarn. Pink and blue flagging is tied to branches, roots and sticks about every hundred yards; go more than about thirty yards without seeing any and backtrack rather than press on. Four boulder fields are crossed on the way up, the first near 3,500 ft and the second near 4,200 ft, which holds snow into summer.
hazards: Unmaintained track with blowdown, brush and faint braids — parties regularly lose it, and it is far less obvious on descent
A moat where the snow meets the rock at the cliff band, which is what actually stops parties
Climbing back out of the wrong gully means steep dirt above a cliff edge — reported as the most dangerous move on the route
Devil's club on the short descending traverse near 5,200 ft
Many pinnacles on the summit ridge; in poor visibility it is hard to tell which is the last and correct one

name: Beyond Redlining
approach: Drive to the Sunrise Mine trailhead (Mountain Loop Highway, Forest Road 4065) and start up the Sunrise Mine Trail. Follow it about 2.5 miles, gaining to roughly 4,300 ft, to the last major switchback before the trail begins its final zigzag up toward Headlee Pass — this is the turnoff point, not the pass itself. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up a cairned traverse heading northeast across open talus toward Vega North Tower (also called Eros Tower). The line of cairns crosses two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees, passing a little above a large flat-topped boulder, which sits near the first stand of trees. This talus traverse is the shared approach for Mile High Club, Marvin's Ear, and Beyond Redlining, so cairns and a boot path are well established in season, but talus can be loose and slow going with a pack. A reliable fresh-water seep is at a red-rock outcrop in the Mile High gully, roughly at the base of the formation — worth topping off here since there's no water higher on the wall. Beyond Redlining's start is on the dark gray face directly above the two largest boulders at the base of the tower, just left of (west of) Mile High Club's start. Expect lingering steep snow against the base in early season, which can make the last stretch of the talus approach and the transition onto rock its own small crux.
descent: Do not rappel Beyond Redlining itself — official route beta explicitly says it is equipped for emergency use but 'not recommended' as a descent line, since the angle and pitch lengths make it a poor rap line that would need two ropes or a 70m rope with awkward hangs. Instead, from the shared summit, descend via Mile High Club's dedicated rappel line, which works with a single 60m rope over 8 rappels: summit rap rings down through P7, P6 (face descent), a short rap on P5 to a ledge, P4 to one of two available anchors, then the tricky 'upper P3' rappel — this one is the most commonly botched: aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line, where a hidden intermediate P3 anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the station; missing it and rapping straight down the vertical face below can leave you well short of the next anchor on a single rope. Below that, a lower-P3 rap drops to a large ledge, then P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base. The first rap station off the summit is set back roughly 8 ft south of the summit bolts and about 4 ft off the ground — easy to walk past if you're not looking for it.
