Saddlebag your rope on the way down to avoid dropping loose rock or gear on parties below; ledges on this face hold loose material. Because Beyond Redlining offers limited bail options low on the route, parties should carry a 70m rope if there's any real chance of needing to retreat mid-climb rather than topping out to the shared summit.
hazards: party-inflicted rockfall risk across multiple pitches
polished, more run-out rock on pitch 3 (rated 'serious for the grade')
route faces west and stays shaded/cold until roughly 1pm
significant snow can linger at the base December-May (one party found ~15-20 ft of snow at the base in late May)
the 55m opening pitch is long and committing before the first real bail option

waysIn.name: Sunrise Mine Trail to the cairned talus traverse
waysIn.season: June to September. This face is west-facing and stays shaded and cold until roughly midday; significant snow can lie at the base from December through May.
waysIn.notes: Sunrise Mine trailhead, then the trail for about two and a half miles through the two unbridged creek crossings and up through forest to the last major switchback before the final zigzags toward the pass — leave the trail there, not at the pass. A cairned traverse then runs northeast across talus toward the tower, crossing two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees and passing a little above a large flat-topped boulder, which sits near the first stand of trees. The boot path is well established in season because three routes share it. Top up water at the seep by the red-rock outcrop in the gully; there is none higher.
hazards: Two unbridged creek crossings in the first mile
Loose talus on the traverse and party-inflicted rockfall across several pitches
West-facing and shaded until around midday, so cold starts are the norm
Steep snow against the base into early summer, which makes the last stretch of talus and the step onto rock its own small crux
The fifty-five-metre opening pitch commits you before any real bail option

name: West Ridge via Wildhorse Creek
approach: From the Whitepine Creek Trailhead (about 2,800 ft), follow Whitepine Creek Trail #1582 up the valley for about 2.5 miles to the junction with Wildhorse Creek Trail #1592. Bear left onto the Wildhorse Creek Trail and climb through forest into the Wildhorse basin to about 5,400 ft, where the trail passes directly west of the summit. Leave the trail here.
descent: Reverse the route: down the summit ledges to below the headwall, back west along the west ridge, then down through the meadows to rejoin the Wildhorse Creek Trail, and out the Whitepine Creek Trail to the car.
hazards: The final ledges to the summit are exposed.
Loose rock and scree on the upper mountain.
Snow lingers on the upper west slopes into July.
A very long day with little water high up late in the season.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Copper Glance Trailhead (3,800–3,810 ft, small pullout signboard, parking for roughly 7 cars) on FR 5130 (Eightmile Creek Road), follow Copper Glance Trail #519. The first ~1.5 miles follows an old jeep track/mining tramway grade (FSR 505) that served the historic Copper Glance claims — a gentle, steady climb through forest. Around 1.5 miles (~5,100 ft) the track passes the ruins of the Copper Glance Mine; the old adits and structures are hazardous and should not be entered. Just past the mine the route narrows to true single-track and fords Copper Glance Creek (~1.6 miles) near an old bridge that has partially collapsed — expect a careful boulder-hop or wet ford, and note the crossing is explicitly not passable for stock. Beyond the creek the trail crosses a stretch of burned-out forest with heavy blowdown that can slow summer travel considerably (early-season snow actually eases this stretch by burying the deadfall). Watch closely for an easy-to-miss, unsigned climbers' path splitting right off the main Copper Glance Trail below Copper Glance Lake/Basin — this is the cutoff onto Isabella Ridge and Big Craggy's southeast ridge, and it's frequently walked past, especially where snow patches obscure the junction. Take this cutoff up through meadows and talus onto Isabella Ridge, then leave maintained tread around 5,900 ft and climb open slopes toward the southeast ridge proper. Around 7,800 ft the angle steepens and the terrain shifts to tedious, loose ('garbage' rock) scree for the final push to the 8,478 ft summit; early-season snow cover on this upper scree is strongly preferred over the bare, ball-bearing talus of late summer. There is no reliable water past Copper Glance Creek, so fill up there (or at Copper Glance Basin/Lake if camping partway). Total car-to-car distance/gain runs roughly 11–12 miles round trip with about 5,600–5,800 ft of gain when West Craggy is tagged in the same push, as most parties do; Big Craggy alone is somewhat shorter but still needs at least 4,700 ft of gain.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no rappelling — retrace the southeast ridge/rib line used on ascent. Favor climber's right on the upper scree and rock band, where footing is comparatively firmer and there's less rockfall exposure onto anyone below; the loose 'garbage' talus here is the descent's main hazard, particularly when dry and off-trail. Several trip reports specifically note that early-season snow cover on this upper section turns the descent into a fast, controlled plunge-step (or glissade in the snow gullies below the ridge), and is generally regarded as easier and safer than picking down the bare, ball-bearing scree of late summer — but check runout on any glissade line before committing, since the gullies feed directly into talus below. Below roughly 7,800 ft, work back down to the small bench and continue the southeast rib downclimb; expect sustained, knee-jarring, loose Class 2–3 terrain most of the way back to where the route rejoins the Copper Glance climbers' path. From there, retrace the approach: back through the burned, blowdown-choked forest, re-ford Copper Glance Creek near the collapsed bridge, pass (but stay out of) the old Copper Glance Mine, and follow the old jeep track back down to the trailhead.
hazards: notably loose rock
exposure on the summit scramble
remote approach
rockfall concentrated in the final 500 ft below the summit
afternoon thunderstorms
early-season snow/glissade hazard hiding rocks

waysIn.name: Copper Glance Trail and the Isabella Ridge cutoff
waysIn.notes: The Craggies are unusual for this corner of the wilderness in that a road and a maintained trail get you most of the way in, which is why the peak sees parties who would not otherwise be this deep. The Copper Glance Trail starts on an old jeep-track mining grade and stays gentle for the first mile and a half to the mine ruins, then narrows to single track, fords the creek near a partly collapsed bridge, and crosses burned forest where blowdown can slow travel badly. Early-season snow buries the deadfall and is generally welcome. The climbing itself is unremarkable: scree, talus and a few hundred feet of genuinely loose blocky ground near the top. Most parties climb West Craggy in the same push, the two being joined by a saddle.
hazards: Very loose rock on the final few hundred feet below the summit
Rockfall onto anyone below on the upper scree
Heavy blowdown through the burned forest on the approach
Creek ford at the collapsed bridge, higher during runoff
No reliable water above the basin crossing
Old mine adits and structures that must not be entered

name: Spindrift Couloir
approach: Walk the nearly wheelchair-accessible nature trail from the Big Four Picnic Area toward the Ice Caves, to the open basin below the North Face. From the trail's end, move right to find a break in the lower cliffs -- straightforward with adequate snow cover, but may require bushwhacking on the far right in sparse-snow years.
descent: The route finishes on the summit ridge, well to the west of the true summit. Descent goes northwest, via rappels and steep downclimbing, to the col between Big Four and Hall Peak; from there, multiple tree-anchored rappels lead back down through the North Face bowl to the base of the face. Careful navigation is essential -- parties have mistakenly descended south instead of northwest in poor visibility.
hazards: Avalanche and spindrift hazard, for which the route is named
Rockfall/icefall potential off the North Face
The ice caves and cliffs at the base of the face are permanently hazardous -- tourists have died there when the caves collapsed on hot days; never approach them
Marginal protection on rotten ice/shale in the upper section

waysIn.name: Ice Caves nature trail to the north face basin
waysIn.season: Winter to early spring — deliberately an early-season line
waysIn.notes:
The shortest approach on this list. Walk the nearly wheelchair-accessible paved nature trail from the Big Four Picnic Area toward the ice caves, and continue to the open basin below the north face. The face rises about 4,000 ft directly above.

From the trail's end move right to find the break in the lower cliff band. With adequate snow cover this is straightforward walking; in a sparse-snow year the only way through is a bushwhack far out to the right.
hazards: Spindrift avalanches down the couloir — the route is named for them
Avalanche hazard on the whole north face in winter
Thin cliff-band break in low-snow years forcing exposed bushwhacking
No retreat once committed to the couloir

name: Going Down Under
approach: Same south-face approach as Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction) to the base of the Beckey-Tate start, then traverse right across overlaps to the route's own start ledge.
descent: From the top of the route, join the standard descent: scramble to the notch just north of the true summit, then follow the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.
hazards: Loose rock typical of the seldom-visited south face
Committing corner pitches with limited bail options mid-route

waysIn.name: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully to the Beckey-Tate base, then traverse right across the overlaps
waysIn.notes:
Same south-face approach as Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully taking the left fork at the high Y-junction to the base of the Beckey-Tate start.

Five pitches, established in 2012.
hazards: No independent ground start; the base is another route's base plus a traverse
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Several routes starting within a short distance on the same wall
Unreliable water late season

name: Kearney-Thomas
approach: Park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20 (roughly Milepost 163, about 1 mile east of Washington Pass). Follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak climbers' path south along Early Winters Creek for roughly 2 miles, then leave the trail to cross the creek and ascend the prominent gully system to the base of the south face, taking the left fork at the high Y-junction. Expect 2.5 to 5 hours of approach time; water is unreliable late season.
descent: As with the neighboring Beckey-Tate line, descend by scrambling to the notch just north of the true summit and following the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.
hazards: Loose approach gully and choss lower on the south face
Long multi-hour approach with unreliable late-season water

waysIn.name: The Hairpin pullout, south along Early Winters Creek about 2 miles, then cross and take the left fork at the high Y-junction
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, roughly milepost 163, about a mile east of Washington Pass. Follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak climbers' path south along Early Winters Creek for roughly 2 miles, then leave the trail to cross the creek and ascend the prominent gully system to the base of the south face.

Expect 2.5 to 5 hours of approach time; water is unreliable late season. Seven pitches.
hazards: A Y-junction where the wrong fork puts you on different ground
2.5 to 5 hours of approach with unreliable water late season
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Three routes starting within about 30 metres on the same wall

name: Skinny Start
approach: Same south-face approach as Kearney-Thomas/Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction) to the base of the south face, then locate the start about 30 meters right of the standard Kearney-Thomas start.
descent: The standard descent is the Beckey-Tate walk-down (scramble to the notch, then the loose gully back to the Hairpin pullout). Rappelling the Beckey-Tate line itself is the other option, but at least one party was unable to find a rappel anchor along the top of that line and instead had to change into rock shoes and make a high traverse to a saddle before descending — budget extra time and be prepared to build your own anchors.
hazards: Dirtier-than-expected rock despite generally clean granite
Rope can jam in thin cracks — manage rope carefully on the thin pitches

waysIn.name: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully, left fork at the Y, then 30 metres right of Kearney-Thomas
waysIn.notes:
Same south-face approach as Kearney-Thomas and Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully taking the left fork at the high Y-junction to the base of the south face.

Three pitches, established in 2012.
hazards: A 30-metre offset from a neighbouring start as the only positional marker
A reported failure to find the expected rappel anchor on the standard descent
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Unreliable water late season

name: Walkabout
approach: Same as Beckey-Tate/Kearney-Thomas: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path south along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the prominent south-face approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction). Expect 2.5-5 hours; water is unreliable late season.
descent: The first-ascent team bivied on the summit after topping out at 2 a.m. and descended the following morning via the Beckey-Tate line — scrambling to the notch just north of the summit, then following the loose scree-and-snow gully back toward the Hairpin pullout (roughly two hours from the summit).
hazards: Committing aid climbing through overhanging, crackless roof terrain low on the route
Long, serious undertaking far from rescue on an obscure face

name: West Face / West Route
approach: From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 (about 1 mile east of Washington Pass, near milepost 163), pick up the cairned climbers' trail on the west side of Early Winters Creek — the same start used for Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak. Follow it roughly 0.5-0.7 mile through open timber to where it meets the edge of a talus/boulder field. Rather than continuing south toward Kangaroo Pass (the Kangaroo Temple line), leave the trail here and cross Early Winters Creek — normally an easy rock-hop, but treat it with respect during peak snowmelt or after rain, since there is no bridge. Once across, the route becomes an open boot-track/light bushwhack through slide alder and slabs, trending east into the basin below Big Kangaroo. Around 6,000 ft, aim for the broad, shallow west-facing gully that leads up toward the notch just north of the summit block, identifiable by a distinct chockstone partway up. The gully is loose underfoot (stay near its edges or on the thin vegetation for better footing rather than the center choss), and narrows with downsloping slabs about halfway — some parties bypass this by favoring the adjacent north-side gully. Rope up below the chockstone: the first of the route's three roped pitches passes it to the notch, the second traverses around the summit block, and the third climbs the summit slab. One-way gain to this point is roughly 2,700 ft over about 2 miles; budget 2.5-4 hours depending on snow and route-finding, longer early season when the gully still holds snow (carry a light axe/crampons through July). Total car-to-car time is commonly 6+ hours.
descent: The route's final move is the crux of the whole outing: an exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old, rusty 1/4-inch bolt to the tiny summit. This is downclimbed or top-roped back to the belay stance rather than rappelled — there's no real anchor up top to rap from, and space on the summit is too small for a stance. From that belay/notch, two slung-block (tat) anchors serve the gully descent: the standard method is one single-rope rappel (a 60m rope is sufficient) using either anchor to get below the steepest, loosest section of the gully; some parties instead break this into two shorter rappels via an intermediate anchor lower down, particularly useful for retrieving gear cached near the chockstone. From the bottom of the rappel(s), downclimb/scree-surf the remaining gully back into the approach basin, re-cross Early Winters Creek, and pick up the climbers' trail back to the Hairpin Turn. Keep a helmet on for the whole descent — the gully sheds loose rock readily, especially with parties above or below.
hazards: exposed, largely unprotected 5.6 summit slab (single old 1/4-inch bolt most parties don't trust)
long, sustained Kangaroo Ridge approach with route-finding through two parallel gullies
west-face gullies often hold snow into July

waysIn.name: The Hairpin turnout, cross Early Winters Creek at the talus edge, then the west gully with the chockstone
waysIn.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 about a mile east of Washington Pass near milepost 163, pick up the cairned climbers' trail on the west side of Early Winters Creek, the same start used for Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak. Follow it roughly 0.5-0.7 mile through open timber to where it meets the edge of a talus and boulder field.

Rather than continuing south toward Kangaroo Pass, which is the Kangaroo Temple line, leave the trail here and cross Early Winters Creek. Normally an easy rock-hop, but treat it with respect during peak snowmelt or after rain; there is no bridge. Once across, the route becomes an open boot-track and light bushwhack through slide alder and slabs, trending east into the basin below Big Kangaroo.

One-way gain to the base of the roped climbing is roughly 2,700 ft over about 2 miles; budget 2.5-4 hours, longer early season. Car-to-car is commonly 6-plus hours.
hazards: An unbridged crossing of Early Winters Creek that runs high in snowmelt
A loose gully that narrows onto downsloping slabs at mid-height
An exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old rusty quarter-inch bolt at the summit
The gully sheds loose rock readily; keep helmets on for the whole descent
Snow in the gully into July in some years

name: East Ridge (Hardscrabble) Route
approach: Start at the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate and walk (or mountain-bike) the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about 7 miles to the boot path for Hardscrabble Lakes, which starts roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake, staying near the inlet — straying left leads into cliff bands. The path from the old road to the lower lake is overgrown but cairned across the talus; fallen trees at each end of the talus make it easy to lose. Above the upper lake expect a brush bash to reach the talus gully, in both directions.
descent: From the summit, retrace the east ridge onto the north-slope granite slab, climb back up to the col, and descend the gully to upper Hardscrabble Lake; follow the inlet-side climbers path back down to the lower lake and rejoin the old road for the multi-mile walk-out.
hazards: The east face/buttress above lower Hardscrabble Lake is steep and cliffy — stay on the inlet-side climbers path
Long, remote approach with no maintained trail for the final stretch to the lakes
Very light foot traffic; do not expect a reliable boot path throughout

waysIn.name: The gated Middle Fork road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Dingford Creek trailhead gate and walk — or mountain-bike, which is the sensible choice — the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about seven miles.

The boot path for the Hardscrabble Lakes leaves roughly half a mile short of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a large fallen log. Follow the climbers' path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake.

About 20 km and 5,300 ft, and very light foot traffic — do not expect a reliable boot path throughout.
hazards: The east face and buttress above lower Hardscrabble Lake are steep and cliffy — stay on the inlet-side path
A long, remote approach with no maintained trail for the final stretch
Very light foot traffic, so no dependable boot path
Early-season snow in the gully to the col
A multi-mile road walk out at the end of a long day

name: North Slope (Dingford) Route
approach: Drive to the Dingford Creek Trailhead gate via Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Rd / FSR 56 (about 18 mi from North Bend; the last several miles are rough gravel, high-clearance recommended). Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 mi to the Hester Lake Trail junction, continue left (east) toward Myrtle Lake (about 2 more miles). From Myrtle Lake, leave the trail and climb steep, increasingly brushy terrain toward Big Snow Lake, then traverse right around Snowflake Lake before ascending gullies/a snow couloir on the mountain's NW flank to the upper rock fields.
descent: Downclimb the same chutes/couloir used on ascent, taking care on crumbly, mossy rock and any residual snow or ice, especially early in the season; traverse back around Snowflake Lake, drop to Big Snow Lake, then pick a line down through brush to Myrtle Lake and follow the Dingford Creek Trail out to the trailhead.
hazards: No maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake; light foot traffic keeps any boot path faint
Steep gullies/chutes above Big Snow Lake can hold snow or ice well into summer
Remote, seldom-visited terrain with real self-rescue implications if injured

waysIn.name: Dingford Creek Trail to Myrtle Lake, then off-trail past Big Snow and Snowflake Lakes
waysIn.season: July to September, best once the gullies and couloir have melted out
waysIn.notes:
Drive to the Dingford Creek trailhead gate via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road / FSR 56, about eighteen miles from North Bend, with the last several miles rough gravel and high clearance recommended.

Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 miles to the Hester Lake Trail junction, then continue left (east) toward Myrtle Lake, about two miles more.

From Myrtle Lake the maintained trail ends. Serious route-finding and bushwhacking start here and failed attempts from losing the line are common.

About 9.7 km and 5,280 ft.
hazards: No maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake, and any boot path stays faint
Steep gullies and chutes above Big Snow Lake holding snow or ice well into summer
Crumbly, mossy rock in the chutes
Remote, seldom-visited terrain with real self-rescue implications
Rough gravel road access with high clearance recommended

name: East Buttress
approach: As for the other routes: Rainy Pass/Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, via Heather Pass and Lewis Lake to Wing Lake camp; the East Buttress is accessed from the east side of the Wing Lake basin rather than the south col or NE ridge notch.
hazards: Loose rock in the gully sections, as on the peak's other routes.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Blackcap sits deep in the Pasayten Wilderness and is reached almost entirely off-trail after a long, multi-day trail approach — there is no short car-to-summit option. The standard approach starts at the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead at Slate Pass (~6,900 ft) on Slate Peak Road, the spur above Harts Pass off FS-5400 and the highest trailhead in Washington reached by road. From the trailhead, follow the Buckskin Ridge Trail over Slate Pass for about 0.9 mile, then take the Whistler Cutoff down into the Middle Fork Pasayten valley to Robinson Creek/Middle Fork Pasayten Trail #478, about 4 miles in. Follow the Middle Fork downstream (north) for about five miles, then climb to Fred's Lake, a reliable water source and the usual first-night camp (about 5 hours trailhead-to-camp at a backpacking pace). A longer alternative starts low at the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the Lost River Road and crosses Robinson Pass into the same valley. Day two, climb from Fred's Lake to 7,100-ft Rolo Pass on the ridge crest above the lake; Lake Doris is a short side trip from here. From Rolo Pass, drop into Upper Eureka Creek (another dependable water source) and cross east into scenic Shellrock Basin, then climb to 7,500-ft Shellrock Pass — a full trail day of roughly 2.5-3 hours from Fred's Lake. Camp is typically made in Shellrock Basin, just below and east of the pass. From camp, leave the trail at Shellrock Pass and traverse SSW across an open, grassy/rocky basin, staying below the cliff bands, to the base of a talus slope; work the left (east) edge of the talus south to a saddle/col just west of the cliff terminus, directly below Blackcap's east face — this off-trail link is about 1-1.5 miles and 1,000-1,500 ft of gain/loss with real route-finding (a steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass often needs to be bypassed on the left in early season — carry an axe if snow persists). From the col, scramble up loose scree and talus on Blackcap's east face to gain the northeast ridge, where the rock transitions to distinctive black hornfels/shale; follow the ridge (staying on its left/south side as terrain allows) on easy Class 2-3 with some exposure and loose rock near the top to the summit. Camp-to-summit is about 5-6 hours round trip. An alternate eastern approach exists via the Monument Creek Trail, leaving it a few miles before Butte Pass where Monument Creek bends west into the open Monument-Blackcap basin, then climbing that basin's cliff band on either flank to reach the same upper mountain — but the Shellrock Pass approach described above is the standard, most-traveled line. Either way this is a serious wilderness undertaking: expect 30-35+ round-trip miles and 3-5 days car-to-car, with the Middle Fork Pasayten River crossing running high and cold in early season and long stretches of trail that can be brushy or storm-damaged in a given year.
descent: This is a scramble with no rappelling — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the black-hornfels summit, downclimb the northeast ridge (Class 2-3, loose in spots) back down to the east-face scree/talus, which is noticeably looser and more hazardous descending than ascending — plan on a slow, controlled downclimb with attention to kicking rock onto anyone below. Continue down the scree/talus to the col, then reverse the off-trail traverse (talus edge, then NNE across the grassy/rocky basin) back over to Shellrock Pass, re-bypassing the snowfield if it was present on the way in, and drop back to camp in Shellrock Basin. From there the return to the trailhead simply reverses the multi-day trail approach: Shellrock Basin to Shellrock Pass, over Rolo Pass, past Fred's Lake, down to and along the Middle Fork Pasayten River, back up the Whistler Cutoff and over Slate Pass, and out to the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead. No technical gear (rope, rack, harness) is needed anywhere on this route; a helmet and trekking poles/ice axe (for any lingering snow near Shellrock Pass) are the only extras worth carrying. This is a full walk-off/downclimb.
hazards: loose talus
long remote Pasayten approach
difficult/high fords of Eureka Creek during snowmelt (historically bridge-less)

waysIn.name: Shellrock Basin camp and the traverse to the east-face col
waysIn.notes: Blackcap is a leg of a multi-day traverse rather than an objective on its own, and the walk in is measured in days, not hours. The usual staging is a camp in Shellrock Basin just below and east of Shellrock Pass, reached over Rolo Pass from Fred's Lake after a long valley approach up the Middle Fork Pasayten. From camp the peak is a half-day round trip on easy ground. Water is at the basin and in upper Eureka Creek and there is none on the mountain. An eastern line exists off the Monument Creek trail into the open Monument-Blackcap basin, but the Shellrock side is the travelled one and the one with a recognisable start.
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the east face, worse descending than ascending
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
Steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass can persist into early summer
High, cold fords of Eureka Creek and the Middle Fork Pasayten in runoff
Days from the nearest road with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
waysIn.notes: From the Robinson Creek trailhead on the Lost River road, climb over Robinson Pass and descend into the Middle Fork Pasayten, joining the standard line up to Freds Lake and over Rolo Pass into Shellrock Basin. It starts much lower than Slate Pass but works when the upper Harts Pass road is not an option, and suits loop trips.
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the east face, worse descending than ascending
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
Steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass can persist into early summer
High, cold fords of Eureka Creek and the Middle Fork Pasayten in runoff
Multi-day approach over Robinson Pass, with the return regaining the pass
Days from the nearest road with no cell coverage
waysIn.whyThisWay: When the upper Harts Pass road is not usable, or for a loop trip, starting from a much lower trailhead and joining the standard line in the Middle Fork valley.

waysIn.name: Monument Creek and the Monument-Blackcap basin
waysIn.notes: Follow the Monument Creek trail toward Butte Pass, and a few miles short of the pass leave it where Monument Creek bends west into the basin between Monument Peak and Blackcap. The lower basin is slow going, but its upper part is open and pleasant, and the peak is climbed from there.
hazards: Slow going in the lower Monument-Blackcap basin
Loose scree and talus on the climb; descending is worse
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
Exposed 5th-class ridge toward Monument Peak; avoid it as a route
Avalanche and cornice terrain on winter approaches
Long, remote approach with no quick escape
waysIn.whyThisWay: For an eastern line off the Monument Creek trail into the open basin below the peak, putting up with slow going lower down instead of staging from Shellrock Basin.

name: Blue's Buttress
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington/Sedro-Woolley, then east on SR-20 through Marblemount and over Rainy Pass and Washington Pass; from Winthrop/Mazama it's a quick 20-30 minute drive west on SR-20 instead. Park in the large pullout at the hairpin turn on SR-20, about a mile east of Washington Pass. Walk south through the boulder field on the climbers' path that heads up the valley toward Kangaroo Pass. After roughly half a mile, leave the path where a drainage comes down off Poster Peak on the right, and follow cairns up it through trees and talus, staying low near treeline rather than traversing high on loose rock, to the foot of Poster Peak's two northeast buttresses. Blue's Buttress is the left-hand (southerly) one, marked by a large roof low down; allow a little over an hour from the car.
descent: From the summit, descend southeast toward Poster Col (the saddle at approximately 7,130 feet) via easy 3rd class terrain. Continue into the steep scree gully below the col, carefully down-climbing loose terrain. If snow is present, boot-ski or carefully descend snowy sections. Contour back to the buttress base and retrace the approach via cairn-marked terrain. Descent typically takes 30 minutes to over an hour depending on conditions and party ability. Use caution on all loose rock and scree.
hazards: Loose rock is prevalent throughout the climb, particularly in lower gully sections and on the descent terrain.
Rock quality deteriorates in lower sections but improves significantly on the ridge crest; route-finding should prioritize solid rock.
The initial gully approach to the ridge has limited protection and difficult, awkward climbing with downsloping holds.
Objective rockfall hazard exists on the descent gully, especially if other parties are climbing higher on the peak.
Snow and ice may be present on lower sections during early season (before mid-June), requiring additional protection and care.

waysIn.name: Hairpin pullout to the Poster Peak drainage
waysIn.notes: Park at the large hairpin-turn pullout on SR-20 about a mile east of Washington Pass — not the Blue Lake Trailhead, which serves the far side of the Liberty Bell group and puts you on the wrong mountain. Take the climbers' path south up the valley toward Kangaroo Pass. About half a mile along, before the path rears up for the pass, a drainage comes down off Poster Peak on the right; leave the path there and follow it up over talus and slab benches toward the two northeast-facing buttresses on the skyline. Reckon on a little over an hour from the car to the rock. Coming out, walk southeast off the summit to the col on the southeast ridge near 7,130 ft, drop the loose gully back to the foot of the buttresses, and pick the cairns back up to the hairpin.
hazards: Considerable loose rock on the buttress crest — the ridge sheds onto anyone below
Talus and slab benches in the approach drainage are slick when wet
Lingering snow in the drainage and in the descent gully into early summer

name: Cascadian Route
approach: Multi-stage approach (~11+ miles): drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then hike to a camp at about 7,000 ft near the North Star-Bonanza col - a full day of travel and approach.
descent: From the Southwest Summit, downclimb/traverse to the Isella Glacier and descend along an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then cross through a notch in the south ridge to regain the North Star-Bonanza col camp.
hazards: Abundant loose rock ('choss') throughout the route.
Difficult retreat/bail options near the summit roof systems.

waysIn.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch
waysIn.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the only ascent on record is late August, and its two neighbours were also climbed in late summer for the driest rock
waysIn.notes:
Same approach as its neighbours and the same camp: drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then about eleven miles of trail and cross-country to a camp near 7,000 ft at the North Star-Bonanza col. It is a full day of travel and approach before anything else happens.

From camp the base is reached over talus. This route is on the west face proper rather than the north-west buttress its two neighbours share, and it tops out just right of the Southwest Summit.

It is sixteen pitches, just over 2,000 ft of net gain and about 2,800 ft of climbing, with a great deal of loose rock and several pitches where the protection is minimal and the holds are portable. Bail options near the summit roof systems are poor.

The descent from the Southwest Summit traverses to the Isella Glacier and follows an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then crosses a notch in the south ridge back to the col camp — two ropes.
hazards: Abundant loose rock over sixteen pitches, with several pitches on minimal protection and portable holds
Poor retreat options near the summit roof systems on a wall with no fixed gear
A descent that crosses the Isella Glacier and a notch in the south ridge, needing two ropes and daylight
Rock quality that varies pitch by pitch, including a choss band low on the route taken at 5.9R

Remoteness on the scale of a three-day weekend before the first pitch, on boat-and-bus access through Lucerne and Holden that has been closed since January 28, 2026 (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-05-26-04, through December 31, 2027)

name: Mary Green Glacier (Standard Route)
approach: From Holden Village (~3,300') walk the gravel road/Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west about 0.9 mile to the signed junction with the Holden Lake Trail and bear right (north). The Holden Lake Trail climbs steadily for about 4 miles through forest, brush, and a few small side-creek crossings (reliable water) to Holden Lake (5,278'), set in a cirque directly below Bonanza's east face — a natural camp and last easy water before things get rougher. From the lake's outlet the tread becomes increasingly faint, skirting the north shore through slide alder and talus (real bushwhacking and route-finding here, especially early season with high water), then climbing a hillside traverse northwest to Holden Pass (6,360'), the standard high camp and last reliable water before committing to the glacier. From the pass, make a rising traverse west along the ridge/slope to a snowfield beneath rock slabs around 7,000–7,300'; scramble the class 3 slabs — start high and right to skirt a waterfall — to gain the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier. All told, roughly 5 miles and ~3,000' gain from Holden Village to high camp, then another ~3,000' of glacier and summit rock above that. Hazards: black flies between 3,000–4,000' and mosquitoes from the lake upward; loose, rockfall-prone gullies below the glacier's retreating margin (stay left/out of the fall line where other parties may be above); and a moat crossing near the top that is usually just a short step across onto rock. From the glacier's northern edge, ascend bearing west along its north (climber's right) edge, then traverse southwest along the base of Bonanza's NE ridge to the glacier's upper corner before crossing the moat.
descent: Reverse the route: down-climb the summit ridge and rocky rib back toward the glacier, staying climber's left of the standard line to dodge rockfall funneling down the gullies. The established descent uses 6–7 fixed rappel stations (horns, flakes, and slung boulders left by prior parties) along the class 3–4 rock band, typically consolidated into about four rappels using a 60m x 8mm rope — a common sequence is one rappel off the east ridge into the upper gully, then three more down through the rock to within roughly 200 feet of the glacier, where you downclimb or walk the rest onto snow. One frequently-used anchor sits on a large boulder/flake at a wet slab lower on the route; multiple trip reports flag it as sketchy and overdue for fresh webbing, so back it up or extend it rather than trusting it outright. Inspect every fixed station before weighting it — Cascades alpine anchors get sun-bleached, chewed by rockfall, or buried season to season. Parties comfortable downclimbing exposed 3rd/easy 4th class can skip some of the raps. Once back on the glacier, recross the moat and descend to Holden Pass camp.
hazards: loose summit rock
crevasses
moat crossing (can become a maze of crevasses after ~July 20)
remote boat-only access
The upper mountain has real rockfall to manage, and a moat/steep snow crossing near the summit ridge is commonly protected with a rope even by parties who scramble the rest unroped

waysIn.name: Holden Village via the Lake Chelan ferry, then Holden Lake and Holden Pass
waysIn.season: Jun-Oct, best early to mid July
waysIn.notes:
Getting to the trailhead is part of the trip and it runs on someone else's timetable: drive to Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry up the lake to the Lucerne landing, then the roughly thirteen-mile bus up to Holden Village at about 3,300 ft. Reservations and a look at the ferry and bus schedules come before anything else in the planning.

From Holden, walk the gravel road and Railroad Creek Trail west about a mile to the signed Holden Lake Trail junction and bear right. That trail climbs steadily about four miles through forest and brush, with small side-creek crossings for water, to Holden Lake at 5,278 ft, in a cirque directly beneath Bonanza's east face — a natural camp and the last easy water.

Past the lake outlet the tread fades. Skirt the north shore through slide alder and talus, which is real bushwhacking and route-finding especially with high water early in the season, then climb a hillside traverse north-west to Holden Pass at 6,360 ft — the standard high camp and the last reliable water before the glacier. That is roughly five miles and three thousand feet from the village.

It is worth going in July in most years: later the glacier breaks up and the problem becomes getting off the ice and onto the rock at all.
hazards: wet, slabby class 3 with a waterfall running through it below the glacier
loose, rockfall-prone gullies below the glacier's retreating margin — keep out of the fall line of parties above
icefall above the slabs
moat at the top of the glacier, which widens through the season
slide alder and vague route-finding past Holden Lake, worst with high water
black flies between about 3,000 and 4,000 ft, mosquitoes from the lake upward
the trip is gated by the ferry and bus schedule, so a delay is not recoverable on the day

name: Southeast Face
approach: From the Boston Basin Trailhead, a pullout on Cascade River Road below the road end (~3,200 ft, roughly mile 21.7), follow the unmaintained but well-established boot path through forest and slide alder, climbing steeply into Boston Basin (~3.2 mi, ~3,100 ft gain). Most parties camp at the basin's high camp (~6,400 ft) to shorten summit day, though the low camp (~5,300 ft) is an option for slower groups. From high camp, an alpine start gets you roped up the Quien Sabe Glacier to the Sahale-Boston col (~8,200 ft), then across the head of the Boston Glacier past the bergschrund to the base of the southeast-side ledges. From there, ascend unroped via loose, sandy 3rd/4th-class ledges on the east/southeast face (to minimize rockfall exposure to parties below) to a crux move just below the summit ridge, then a short scramble to the top. Hazards: crevasse danger on the Quien Sabe/Boston Glacier crossing (worsens through the season as the bergschrund opens), loose rock on the face's ledges and crux, and typical North Cascades afternoon rockfall/softening — an alpine start is standard.
descent: Descend by reversing the approach to the summit ridge, then rappel rather than downclimb the loose upper face: from the summit, walk a few feet toward Sahale to the first rappel sling/station. Three rappels down the southeast/east face bring you back to the snow at the head of the Boston Glacier, near the base of the Sahale–Boston col. Multiple independent trip-report accounts describe the anchors as roughly 25m apart station-to-station but recommend carrying 60m ropes (used doubled, ~30m per pitch) so you are never left short between stations — bring extra webbing, since the fixed slings, while described as well-positioned and currently in good condition, are natural/gear anchors (slung horns and blocks, not bolts) and are exactly the kind of aging tat worth backing up before weighting. After the third rappel, reverse the glacier traverse back up to the Sahale–Boston col and descend the Quien Sabe Glacier to camp in Boston Basin, then the boot path back to the trailhead. Hazards on descent: rockfall in the rappel line (helmet on, and be mindful of parties above/below), softening snow bridges on the glacier walk-off in the afternoon, and the mountain's generally loose, exposed rock — Boston has a real fatality history and the descent should not be treated casually.
hazards: notoriously loose and rotten rock
rockfall onto and within the party
exposure on fourth-class steps
afternoon thunderstorms

Crevassed glacier approach up the Quien Sabe from Boston Basin — the big crevasses are low on the glacier, and the direct line through them runs to about 45° and is very exposed, so most parties take the left side and traverse in beneath Sharkfin Tower. The snow traverse on the col to the summit block is short but exposed, and wants axe and crampons.

waysIn.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to the Sahale-Boston col, then the connecting ridge
waysIn.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft at about mile 21.7 of Cascade River Road, the unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and slide alder into Boston Basin, roughly 3.2 miles and 3,100 ft. Most parties camp at high camp near 6,400 ft; the low camp near 5,300 ft works for slower groups. Sahale Glacier Camp on the other side of the ridge serves the same objective for parties coming over Cascade Pass.

An alpine start is standard. Rope up the Quien Sabe Glacier — the big crevasses are low on the glacier and the direct line through them runs to about 45 degrees and is very exposed, so most parties take the left side and traverse in beneath Sharkfin Tower. Later in the season, end-run the bergschrund below the col by traversing climber's right, then cut back up-left above it to gain the Sahale-Boston Col at about 8,200 ft.

From the col the route follows the connecting ridge toward Boston: flat at first, then widening onto loose rock, staying generally right and on the crest.

The difficulty here is the rock quality, not the grade. This peak has a real fatality history and the descent — three rappels off fixed slings down the southeast side — should not be treated casually.
hazards: Crevasses on the Quien Sabe, with a potentially poorly bridged bergschrund below the col that worsens through the season
Notoriously loose and rotten rock, with rockfall onto and within the party
Essentially unprotectable class 4 with real exposure on the knife-edge section
A short but exposed snow traverse on the col that wants axe and crampons
Aging natural rappel anchors on the descent — slung horns and blocks, not bolts

name: Boving-Christensen
approach: Reached via the same Core Enchantments approach as the other south-face lines: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft), then the south-end boulder field and Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree — the approach's crux, hazardous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face, roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country navigation over slabs and talus for the final stretch.
descent: Same north-side descent as the neighboring Solid Gold and Energizer Bunny lines: locate the shared rap anchors on the north side of the ridge and make one full-length rappel (a 60m rope is standard) down to easier ground, then scramble/downclimb roughly 30 minutes back around to the base of the south face. Anchors here are natural (slung blocks/chockstones, webbing/tat) rather than bolted, and per recent forum reports have been periodically rebuilt as old tat accumulates — back up any worn-looking station.
hazards: Some loose/dirty rock reported on the long second pitch.

waysIn.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, then a hundred feet right of the left-flank classic
waysIn.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, the crux of the walk in, dangerous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face — roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way, the last stretch unmarked over slabs and talus.

Four pitches, about 450 ft: a short crack and slab to a corner, a long exposed and somewhat dirty face-crack pitch, a corner with a bouldery move, and a finishing fingers-to-hands pitch to the ridge.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
Long, exposed, somewhat dirty second pitch
Natural non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side; check slings and tat
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Afternoon thunderstorms with a long walk back over the pass
Avalanche-prone approach in shoulder season

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
waysIn.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the face below Prusik Pass. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.
hazards: Long approach, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain
Avoids the Aasgard Pass scree but still crosses unmarked slab and talus to the face
Long, exposed, somewhat dirty second pitch
Natural non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side; check slings and tat
Afternoon thunderstorms with a long way back to the trailhead
waysIn.whyThisWay: To avoid the loose, snow-prone grind of Aasgard Pass, trading roughly two extra miles and a thousand feet of gain for a gentler, more gradual walk.

name: Southwest Ridge (Hemlock Pass)
approach: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappels and no fixed anchors. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose Class 3 summit block carefully, facing in where it is steep, then return across the talus and down the ridge to Hemlock Pass, keeping to the ascent line around the cliff bands rather than cutting down the fall line. From the pass, follow the Denny Creek Trail back down to the trailhead. The steep gully between Bryant and Chair Peak on the Source Lake side is a separate line and an avalanche path in winter and spring; it is not a descent from this route.
hazards: loose scree
lingering snow early season
loose, exposed summit block with rockfall from parties above

waysIn.name: Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then the ridge
waysIn.season: Late July to September for a dry scramble; earlier the ridge and talus hold snow and an axe is needed
waysIn.notes: The standard summer approach. From the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft), reached from I-90 Exit 47 by Denny Creek Road and FR 5830, follow the Denny Creek Trail #1014 toward Melakwa Lake past waterfalls and up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft of gain. Leave the trail at the pass for the ridge on the right.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall on the summit block; parties above can knock rocks down
Lingering snow on the ridge and talus early in the season; axe needed
Brush in the notch below the talus once the snow has gone
Exposure on the north side of the summit block
Loose scree on the upper slopes

waysIn.name: Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the Bryant-Chair gully
waysIn.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
waysIn.notes: A steeper alternative from the Alpental side, better known as a winter and spring snow climb than as a summer scramble. From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits left (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.
hazards: Gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring
Loose scree, centre and left markedly worse than the right
Gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow requiring axe and crampons
Exposed, loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when dry
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from the Alpental side or wanting a steeper snow line, early in the season while the gully still holds snow and an axe and crampons are needed.

name: South Ridge
approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk) at the end of the Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 (~2,800 ft), follow Buck Creek Trail #1513. The trail splits from the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 within the first mile and climbs steadily through forest; around mile 2.75-3 it crosses the upper Chiwawa River, where there is no longer a footbridge; look for a log crossing near the old bridge site and have a wading backup plan, since the river runs fast and deep in early season. Above the crossing the trail is a long, fairly shadeless, grinding ascent (mosquitoes/black flies are heavy in July) through forest and then subalpine meadow along the flank of Middle Ridge, opening into increasingly good wildflower and Glacier Peak views as you climb. At roughly 9.25-10 miles and about 3,000-3,300 ft of gain, the trail tops out at Buck Creek Pass (~5,800-5,900 ft) - one of the most scenic passes in the Cascades, with a reliable spring near the pass for water (last dependable source before the basin). Beyond the pass there is no maintained trail: pick up the well-used climbers'/boot path that switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap and the High Pass Trail junction, then leave that path to contour and traverse west/southwest, staying below Liberty Cap, into the upper basin below Buck Mountain's south and west aspects (Louis Creek Basin, ~6,700 ft) - the standard camp for a two-day trip. Follow the ridge crest through Class 2-3 terrain (stepping to locally 3-4 near a horn/gendarme close to the true summit) on loose, rubbly, slabby schist to the top; the summit crest has several bumps within feet of each other, so take care identifying the true high point. Primary approach hazards: rockfall/loose schist (helmet recommended, especially with parties above or below), the river crossing in high water, no reliable water source between the pass and the basin in a dry year, and route-finding above Buck Creek Pass since the climbers' path is intermittent. An alternate historic approach reaches Buck Mountain via Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa Valley, used for longer traverses.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved on the standard South Ridge route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 (locally 3-4 near the summit horn) loose, rubbly schist back down the ridge crest to the low-angle snowfield/basin around 7,400 ft, then descend the pumice and talus slopes back to the Louis Creek Basin camp (~6,700 ft). From there, traverse back east below Liberty Cap to rejoin the boot path down to Buck Creek Pass, and finish on the maintained Buck Creek Trail #1513 for the roughly 9.25-10 mile, ~3,000-3,300 ft descent back to the Trinity Trailhead. Trip reports on this route put summit-day round trip from a Buck Creek Pass/Louis Creek Basin camp at roughly 4 hours; given a car-to-car round trip of roughly 30 miles, most parties treat this as an overnight (camp at Buck Creek Pass or the upper basin) rather than a single push, though strong parties have done it in a long day. The main descent hazard is the same loose schist encountered on the way up - downclimbing loose rock is generally more dangerous than ascending it, so descend deliberately, test holds, and keep the group tight (or move one at a time) through the Class 3-4 band near the summit to avoid kicking rock onto climbers below. Rappels: 0.
hazards: loose rock
ridge exposure
lingering snow on approach
loose black schist on the upper scramble slopes
short Class 3-4 step near a rock horn just below the true summit
stream crossings on the Buck Creek Trail approach
afternoon thunderstorms possible in late summer

waysIn.name: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse from the Berge saddle crosses steep heather that is nasty when wet, and holds snow into summer
waysIn.notes:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. Fill up with water there — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.
hazards: Burn scar on the lower Buck Creek trail: hot, exposed, with blowdown
No water for four miles beyond Buck Creek Pass on a fully sun-exposed ridge
Hard snowfields at High Pass where crampons are worth having
Waterfall slabs below the traverse line if you lose too much height; steep heather ledges at the Berge saddle are sketchy when wet
Loose, rubbly schist on the summit crest; a fatal fall is on record
Short Class 3-4 step near a rock horn just below the summit
Afternoon thunderstorms possible in late summer

waysIn.name: Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley
waysIn.notes: Ford the Chiwawa River at the Little Giant trailhead, climb steeply over Little Giant Pass and drop into the Napeequa valley. Go upvalley, then leave the trail at Louis Creek and climb its brushy left side past a waterfall into the basin around 6,400 ft on the peak's southwest side. The river ford can be deep and swift in early summer.
hazards: Fording the Chiwawa River at the trailhead; it can be deep and swift in early summer
Steep climb over Little Giant Pass into the Napeequa valley
Leaving the trail at Louis Creek: brushy slope beside a waterfall, off-trail
Loose, slabby schist on the upper scramble slopes
Short Class 3-4 step near a rock horn just below the summit
Lingering snowfields into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms possible in late summer
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a more direct way to the Napeequa side than the long High Pass traverse, best when the Chiwawa River is low enough to ford safely.

name: Southwest Slope via Marmot Pass
approach: From the Upper Big Quilcene Trailhead (~2,650 ft, end of FR-2750), the route follows the Upper Big Quilcene River Trail #833. The first 2.5 miles are an easy, mostly rolling grade through old-growth cedar and hemlock forest with the Big Quilcene River alongside you the whole way — this stretch is your last reliable, easy-access water for a while and there are no fords, just a trail paralleling the river. At about mile 2.5 you reach Shelter Rock Camp (~3,600 ft), a designated camp with water access. Past it, around mile 3.5, the trail pulls away from the river and climbs a sustained, steeper 3/4-mile pitch of switchbacks — the single steepest, most sustained grade on the approach — then continues climbing through subalpine forest and opens into meadows around mile 4.5 at Camp Mystery (~5,300 ft), the last camp and last dependable water source before the pass (treat before drinking). From Camp Mystery it's about another 0.5 mile of open meadow hiking to Marmot Pass (~6,000 ft) at mile 5, a major trail junction where the Tubal Cain Trail forks off toward Buckhorn Lake Camp/the old Tubal Cain Mine, and the main trail continues over the pass toward Home Lake and the Dungeness Trail. Buckhorn's summit route turns right (north) here onto the Tubal Cain Trail for only a short distance, then leaves it for the unsigned climbers'/boot path that climbs right up the open ridge crest roughly 1 mile and 900–1,000 ft of gain to the southwest (higher) summit. It's not an official trail — expect braided boot paths through heather and talus, a few spots where you'll want hands for balance, and a short, easy scramble onto the large boulder that forms the true high point. Route-finding is straightforward in clear weather (stay near the ridge crest) but the braided paths and cliffy drop-offs on the north side make it easy to wander off-line in fog or whiteout, so a GPS track or careful attention to the ridgeline is worthwhile. Lingering snow patches near Camp Mystery and the upper ridge are possible into early summer; a light axe/microspikes can help in that window, though by mid-summer the route is dry scree, talus, and heather.
descent: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the boot path off the summit block, follow the ridge-crest climbers' trail back down to Marmot Pass (watch footing on the loose scree/talus sections — they're more tedious to downclimb than to ascend, and the braided paths can tempt you off-route, especially in poor visibility), then drop back onto the maintained Trail #833 through Camp Mystery, Shelter Rock Camp, and the forest to the trailhead. This is a standard walk-off/scramble descent — no technical downclimbing and no rappelling anywhere on the route. The only sustained knee-punishing stretch is the steep 3/4-mile switchback section between Shelter Rock Camp and Camp Mystery; otherwise it's a straightforward, well-graded trail hike back to the car.
hazards: Loose, rotten rock and scree on the final ~1 mile above Marmot Pass, with rockfall risk to parties below
Lingering snow/ice on the summit slope and at Marmot Pass, often into mid-July, plus snow bridges over the creek crossing below Camp Mystery in early season
Route-finding above Marmot Pass on the open, cairned-but-unmaintained boot path in poor visibility
Habituated, salt-seeking mountain goats at Marmot Pass and on both summits — keep distance and don't let them approach for sweat or urine
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning exposure on the open ridge and summit block in summer
Long, mostly waterless final stretch — Camp Mystery is the last dependable water source before the pass and summit

waysIn.name: Upper Big Quilcene Trail #833 over Marmot Pass
waysIn.notes: An easy river grade through old growth for the first two and a half miles to Shelter Rock Camp, then a sustained switchbacking pitch up to the open meadows at Camp Mystery — the last dependable water before the pass and the summit. Habituated goats work the pass and both summits and will approach for salt; keep your distance and pee well off the trail.
hazards: Loose scree and rotten rock above the pass, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow at the pass and on the summit slope into mid-July
Braided, unmaintained boot paths that are easy to lose in fog
Cliffy drop-offs on the north side of the summit ridge
Long waterless final stretch above Camp Mystery

name: Southwest Face / Southwest Slopes
approach: Start from the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road/FR-15. Take the maintained Cascade Pass Trail, which switchbacks through old-growth forest and then traverses subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at 3.7 mi / ~1,700 ft gain. From the pass, pick up the Sahale Arm Trail heading north/climber's-right: it climbs steadily through heather meadows, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier, ending at Sahale Glacier Camp (~7,600 ft) — 5.9 mi and ~3,940 ft gain one-way from the trailhead, and the standard high camp/base for the route (NPS permit and bear-canister required; camp only in the designated sites at the glacier's edge). Reliable water is available at camp from snowmelt/the glacier's edge early season; carry a stove or filter since Sahale Arm itself is dry above the meadows. From camp the route continues off-trail: descend Sahale Peak's south ridge on class 1-2 rock, then down a short class 3 step to a ~6,800 ft notch, and traverse roughly 2 miles across Horseshoe Basin (6,600-6,800 ft) on talus, slabs, and lingering snow, passing near the old Davenport Mine site (~7,000 ft) to reach the base of Buckner's southwest face. This basin traverse is exposed to rockfall and can require an axe/crampons for steep snow patches into midsummer — start early to avoid afternoon softening and thunderstorm exposure. From the base, climb steepening southwest-facing snowfields toward a distinctive 'cowskull-shaped' snowfield high on the face (the key navigational landmark, described by climbers as looking like a ghost early season); ascend a snow chute and then the cowskull itself, where the angle steepens enough that many parties place running-belay pickets. Above the snow, step off, remove crampons, and grovel up loose scree/rubble to the summit ridge, finishing with about 100 ft of class 2-3 rock scrambling to the true summit. Most parties take 2-3 days car-to-car given the ~20-mile round trip and 7,400 ft of gain, though strong parties have done it in one very long day.
descent: Descend the same southwest-slopes line used on ascent — this is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb the scree/rubble and re-descend the cowskull snowfield and chute on the fall line to about 7,200 ft; steep snow here is typically managed by facing in and plunge-stepping or downclimbing with an ice-axe self-belay, and less experienced parties often protect it with a running belay on pickets. Continue down and traverse right to re-cross Horseshoe Basin on the broad ledge system at 6,200-6,400 ft (passing back near Davenport Mine), then ascend a short ~100 ft snow finger to regain the rounded ridge above the toe of Sahale's south ridge. From there, scramble back up the class 3 step and class 1-2 south ridge to Sahale Glacier Camp, and descend the Sahale Arm/Cascade Pass Trail 5.9 miles back to the Cascade Pass Trailhead. The main descent hazards are loose scree/rubble near the summit and sustained steep snow on the cowskull section (self-arrest skill required); no technical rope work is needed in normal summer conditions.
hazards: loose scree
rockfall
steep early-season snow

waysIn.name: Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin to the cowskull snowfield
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road. The maintained Cascade Pass trail switchbacks through old growth and traverses subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass at 5,400 ft, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft. From the pass take the Sahale Arm trail north through heather meadows, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier and Sahale Glacier Camp near 7,600 ft — 5.9 miles and about 3,940 ft from the trailhead, and the standard base. NPS permit and bear canister required; camp only in the designated sites. Sahale Arm above the meadows is dry, so carry water or a filter.

From camp the route goes off-trail and downhill first: descend Sahale Peak's south ridge on class 1-2 rock, then a short class 3 step into a notch near 6,800 ft, and traverse roughly two miles across Horseshoe Basin on talus, slabs and lingering snow, passing near the old Davenport Mine around 7,000 ft, to reach the base of the southwest face.

Most parties take two to three days for the roughly 20-mile round trip and 7,400 ft of gain, though strong parties have done it in one very long day.
hazards: A steep, snow-filled cleft on Sahale's south ridge that must be downclimbed, exposed and fall-prone on firm early-season snow
Rockfall across the Horseshoe Basin traverse, which is loose and easy to lose the line on in both directions
Cliff bands below the basin ledge system — stay on the mid-elevation line rather than dropping
Steep snow on the cowskull with wet-slide potential in the afternoon; many parties run a picket belay
Loose scree and rubble above the snow, all the way to the summit ridge
An axe and crampons needed for steep snow patches into midsummer

name: Southwest Slopes
approach: From the Entiat River Trailhead (3,150 ft, end of Entiat River Road), follow the Entiat River Trail #1400, a well-graded but increasingly rough valley trail that parallels the Entiat River the entire way. At 2.2 miles (3,480 ft) the Anthem Creek Trail #1435 splits off; the crossing at 2.5 miles is on a solid wooden bridge. At 3.6 miles (3,745 ft) pass the Cow Creek Meadows/Myrtle Lake Trail #1404 junction, then the Larch Lakes Trail #1430 at 4.7 miles (3,780 ft), Snowy Creek Meadows around 6.1 miles, and the Emerald Park Trail #1230 junction at 6.2 miles (4,000 ft). Miles 6-12 cross repeated burn zones from the Tinpan (2006), Wolverine (2015) and Duncan Ridge (2014) fires — expect an exposed, dry, dusty tread with little shade. At 8.2 miles (4,330 ft) pass the Ice Creek Trail #1405 junction, and reach Entiat Meadows proper around 11 miles (4,600 ft), a good camp with reliable water. Continue past the Cool Creek Trail #1431 junction at 13.3 miles (5,060 ft) into upper Entiat Meadows; the trail grows faint and brush/deadfall-choked above about 14 miles as it nears timberline (roughly 14.5-14.8 miles, ~5,100 ft), the usual base camp for the peak. From camp, leave the trail and climb the open, south-facing slope/rib system directly below Buckskin's summit — this is a broad old avalanche path; the rib closest to camp carries the least brush and gives the most direct line, while an old, badly overgrown boot path toward the east ridge is generally not worth chasing due to extensive deadfall. Ascend scree and heather (loose, will be slick when wet) roughly 2,000-2,800 ft to gain the east ridge around 7,200-7,900 ft, then follow the ridge crest — narrow and blocky in spots with minor gendarmes — the final few hundred feet to the 8,127 ft summit. Water is reliable along the entire valley trail (Entiat River, Anthem Creek at 2.2 mi, Snowybrushy Creek around 5.2 mi, plus seasonal side streams) but there is no dependable water above the meadows once you leave the trail, aside from early-season snowmelt. Main approach-specific hazards: heat/sun exposure through the burn sections, navigation through deadfall on the upper trail and on any attempt at the old east-ridge boot path, and loose, ball-bearing scree and wet heather on the open slope below the ridge.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, follow the east ridge back down to roughly 7,200-7,900 ft, then drop off the ridge onto the same south-facing rib/gully used on the way up, picking your way down through loose scree and heather (roughly 3,000 ft of scree plus slick heather) back to the upper Entiat Meadows camp/trail. From there it's a straightforward but long reverse of the Entiat River Trail #1400 (roughly 14.5-15 miles) back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no technical rappelling involved — rope and anchor gear are not part of a normal summer ascent. The scree and heather are noticeably looser and more slippery on the way down than going up, and the burned, faint upper stretch of trail plus any deadfall-choked side paths are the main route-finding hazards on the way out; give yourself enough daylight given the ~15-mile, 5,000 ft round-trip scale of the day. In June a dry rib beside the snow gully leads back to the meadow, with only a short stretch of alder to push through.
hazards: loose scree and rockfall on the ridge and gully
corniced summit ridge with loose gendarmes near the top (stay off the crest)
steep, icy snow on the south-facing approach slope into early summer
long remote trail approach with no cell coverage - not a boat/ferry access route

waysIn.name: Entiat River Trail #1400 to Entiat Meadows
waysIn.season: Mid-July through September once the meadows melt out. In early season the south side holds firm snow and the final ridge can be corniced, turning this into a genuine mountaineering objective.
waysIn.notes: This is the long east-side valley approach, not a boat-access trip. From the road-end trailhead follow Entiat River Trail #1400 up-valley, staying on #1400 at each junction in turn — Anthem Creek, Cow Creek and Myrtle Lake, Larch Lakes, Emerald Park, and Ice Creek. Refill at the reliable creeks in the middle miles, because the long stretch above them crosses repeated burn scars with almost no shade and no water. The valley opens into Entiat Meadows and travel slows through downed timber; step over it where you can, since the detours around it are what lose the tread. Past the Cool Creek junction the trail grows faint and choked with brush and deadfall as it nears timberline; keep going to the open clearing, which is the last dependable water and the camp that keeps the summit day short.
hazards: Heat and sun exposure through the long burn sections with no shade and no water
Heavy deadfall on the upper trail, where the detours around downed timber are what lose the tread
Loose, ball-bearing scree and slick wet heather on the open south face
Rockfall on the open slope — keep in close under the buttress
Cornices and minor gendarmes on the narrow blocky crest into early summer
The whole face is exposed with nowhere to shelter from afternoon storms

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Start at the Stevens Pass PCT-South trailhead (large lot on the south side of US 2, ~4,060 ft, just east of the ski area buildings). Follow the Pacific Crest Trail south; the trail climbs gradually through forest and past Lake Susan Jane, staying high above Nason Creek before working into the Icicle Creek drainage. At roughly 4.5-5 miles from the trailhead, watch for the signed junction with the Icicle Creek Trail (leave the PCT here). Follow the Icicle Creek Trail around Josephine Lake and down past its outlet, about 3.2 miles, to the junction with Chain Lakes Trail #1569. Turn onto Chain Lakes Trail and climb steeply — about 2.5 miles and 1,800-2,000 ft of gain through forest, brush, and talus benches — to the Middle/Upper Chain Lakes basin (~5,700 ft), the last reliable water and the standard base camp for the peak; tank up here, as there is no dependable water above the lakes. From camp, leave the maintained trail and go cross-country around the north/west shore of Upper Chain Lake, then ascend the huge white talus of the northwest-facing gully on the peak's west side to a notch between two sub-summits — footing is loose here and rockfall onto parties below is a real hazard, so group up in the gully. From the notch, scramble south to the base of the summit block. The final pitch to the top is Class 2-3 scrambling on solid granite; the easiest line works around the right (east/south) side of the summit block rather than the left, finishing with an exposed but short Class 3 step and mantle onto the summit. Beyond Chain Lakes the route is entirely unmarked cross-country travel, so route-finding competence, a map/GPX track, and comfort on loose talus and heather slopes are required; the upper mountain is fully exposed to afternoon thunderstorms with no bail-out shelter.
descent: Reverse the ascent line exactly. Downclimb the summit block using the same Class 2-3 moves in reverse — staying on the right (east/south) side is easier and less exposed than the left — then descend from the notch down the loose scree/talus couloir back to Chain Lakes camp (watch footing and any parties below you — this gully sheds rock easily), then follow Chain Lakes Trail #1569 downhill, pick up the Icicle Creek Trail, climb back up to the PCT junction, and follow the PCT north back to the Stevens Pass trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no rappelling on the standard route: 0 rappels. Note that a separate, harder line on the same peak — the technical South Ridge route used by parties doing the full Bullseye Traverse, which ropes up for Class 4-5.8 climbing to reach the true summit gap between Bull's Tooth and the adjacent 'Bullfinch' pinnacle — does use two to three short (~20-30 ft) rappels off horns, trees, and slung blocks to get back down that exposed ridge crest; that gear/anchor style does not apply to the standard scramble described here, which avoids the technical ridge entirely via the couloir and a downclimb.
hazards: exposed Class 3 summit tower
loose rock
long approach via Stevens Pass / Icicle Creek / Chain Lakes Trail
steep, unswitchbacked ~2,000 ft climb into the Chain Lakes basin with loose tread
summit-naming ambiguity -- confirm you're headed for the Class 3, 6,840+ ft high point and not the harder 6,680+ ft rock fang (Class 4-5, rappel required) that is also sometimes called Bulls Tooth

waysIn.name: Stevens Pass crest trail to Chain Lakes and Bullseye Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July to early October, once the basin and the couloir have melted out.
waysIn.notes: From the large lot on the south side of the highway at the pass, follow the crest trail south past Lake Susan Jane and into the Icicle Creek drainage, then take the signed Icicle Creek Trail down toward the head of the valley and turn up Chain Lakes Trail #1569. That trail climbs steeply and without switchbacks through forest, brush and talus benches into the Chain Lakes basin near 5,700 ft, which is the last reliable water and the standard camp. From camp the climb goes cross-country around Upper Chain Lake and up the couloir above it.
