Note that the trail pass between the Chain and Doelle basins is a separate feature reached by trail, and it is the jumping-off point for a different and much harder summit rather than for this one.
hazards: Lower slopes are a deceptively complex mix of steep heather, mossy slabs, brush and short cliff bands
Loose footing in the couloir with a real rockfall risk onto parties below — group up rather than string out
The last hundred feet turns looser and sandier than the talus below it
No dependable water above the Chain Lakes
Entirely unmarked cross-country travel beyond the lakes, with no cairned or established line
The upper mountain is fully exposed to afternoon thunderstorms with no bail-out shelter

name: North Face
approach: From the SR-20 pullout (~4,310 ft, near milepost 166, about 3.75 mi east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain), a boot path drops down through loose talus to the east into forest — this is the trailhead for the shared Burgundy Col approach (there's no numbered Forest Service trail; it's an established but unofficial boot path). A short way in, pass a wilderness trail-register box, then ford Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft (can run swift and cold in early season). From the creek, the path climbs steadily east through forest and then open slopes, gaining roughly 2,200 ft to a broad, flat bench at ~6,460 ft that fits a dozen-plus tents and is the natural approach midpoint and best high camp. Beyond the bench, the trail climbs and traverses loose scree gullies below Burgundy's northwest aspect before a final, cairn-marked stretch of notoriously unstable 'ball-bearing' scree over slab (careful class 2, worse on the way down) up to Burgundy Col at roughly 7,770–7,800 ft, the narrow notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. Total is about 3 miles and 3,500–4,000 ft of gain one-way to the col, with the North Face route starting essentially right above it — the route and first pitch are visually obvious once you're at the col. Water sources: Early Winters Creek near the start, a small trickle on the trail below the col, and occasionally a patch of hard snow/ice on the col's east side late-season. The main approach hazards are the creek ford in early season and the loose scree below the col, which is prone to kicking rockfall onto climbers below — travel tightly grouped and be deliberate with foot placement on that final pitch.
descent: From the summit, the descent is 5 double-rope rappels down the face back to Burgundy Col, then a reversal of the approach. Specifically: R1 (~40m) from a large, heavily slung boulder at the summit down the middle of the upper face to a bolted anchor on a ledge; R2 (~55m) from the bolts down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch — traverse the ledge to a constriction where slings back up the next anchor; R3 (~55m) from that constriction down more lichen-covered rock to a horn with a blue sling (climber's right of the ascent line); R4 (~40m) from that horn down to broad, scree-covered upper ledges — pull the rope carefully here, as there's real potential to snag it on the ledge system; R5 (~60m) down over the lower scramble terrain, landing back at Burgundy Col where the route starts. Double 60m ropes are the standard setup; parties have gotten down with a single 60–70m rope and some added downclimbing between stances (more, shorter rappels than the five double-rope ones; one party logged 9-10), but that's tighter and involves more exposed downclimbing on loose terrain. Anchors are a mix of slung natural features (boulder, horn) and fixed bolts/webbing — inspect webbing before weighting it, since it's exposed to UV and can be old. Once at the base of the last rappel, reverse the Burgundy Col approach (down the loose scree, then the boot path past the flat bench and creek crossing) back to the highway pullout.
hazards: loose rock on the spire
exposed belays
long committing approach to the Wine Spires

waysIn.name: Burgundy Col in a single push
waysIn.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, roughly four miles east of Washington Pass and looking straight across the valley at Silver Star Mountain. There is no numbered Forest Service trail here — the whole thing is an established boot path.

Scramble down the embankment past cairns. The first stretch is loose, scree-covered talus before it settles into a proper path. Cross Early Winters Creek on one of the logs; the logjam shifts year to year, so look up and down stream for the best one, and expect a cold, pushy ford in early season.

On the far bank the path winds through forest for about a quarter of a mile, then turns straight uphill between two small creeks and climbs relentlessly. At about 6,460 ft the angle relents at a broad flat bench — big enough for a dozen tents and the obvious rest stop.

Above the bench the path climbs and traverses loose scree gullies before a final cairned stretch of very unstable scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. That is roughly 3,700 ft above the creek. That last scree is worse on the way down than the way up.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — logs shift, and the ford is cold and swift in early season
extremely unstable ball-bearing scree over slab on the final stretch to the col — this is the section that kicks rocks onto whoever is below, so travel close together
loose talus on the initial drop from the highway
very large gain for a day trip; most parties camp
waysIn.whyThisWay: When doing the col and the climb in one long day without carrying overnight gear to the bench camp, at the price of a heavy pack on the loose scree.

waysIn.name: Camp at the 6,460 ft bench
waysIn.notes:
The usual way this is done. Walk the same line from the milepost 166 pullout — down the loose talus embankment, across Early Winters Creek on logs, through the forest and then steeply up between the two small creeks — and stop at the broad flat bench at about 6,460 ft, which holds a dozen or more tents and is the natural halfway point. There is usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby.

Next morning you carry only what you need for the col and the route, which makes the loose scree above the bench substantially less unpleasant. Reckon on the bench being the last flat ground and the last reliable water.
hazards: the direct-looking gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
loose scree over slab on the traverse into the col
no reliable water above the bench
rockfall onto parties below on the final approach

name: North Route
approach: Park at the Dingford Creek Trailhead, where Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FS Road 56) is gated to vehicles — the last few miles of FS 56 are pitted with potholes and washboard, so high-clearance is strongly recommended — then walk or bike about 7.5 mi of closed road to its old end at the former Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead (Trail #1030). Do not follow the maintained Dutch Miller Gap trail; instead ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River roughly 300 ft upstream of the trailhead to its true-right (north) bank. Early-season and post-snowmelt (roughly June) this ford can run thigh-deep and cold — scout upstream for a braided or log crossing if flows are high. Once across, climb the boulder/talus field directly above the river for about 400 vertical feet until you hit a rock band. At the cliff, angle left (west) into a brushy gully thick with salmonberry and black currant — expect real bushwhacking here, not a trail. Follow the gully up into timber around 3,900 ft, then traverse upward through the trees until you break out onto open talus. From the talus, work up and climber's-left toward the low notch/pass beside Point 5,841, which separates Burnt Boot's summit block from the peak immediately west — this notch is the key route-finding target and where the described 'heather/cedar benches' sit. Above roughly 5,400–5,800 ft, pick a line through talus and boulders to avoid the steepest snow; the final ~200 vertical feet below the pass typically holds a firm, sustained snow ramp well into summer, and an ice axe (crampons/microspikes in early season) is required for this section — it is genuine self-arrest terrain. From the pass, a short class 3–4 ridge traverse leads to the summit. From the ford the summit is roughly 2 mi one way, with nearly all the elevation gain packed into the final two miles above the river. There is no reliable water once you leave the river, aside from occasional early-season snowmelt trickles near the pass. Principal hazards: the river ford itself, sustained brush in the lower gully, loose talus/scree on the upper slopes, and the steep snow ramp below the pass. Near the top of the summit-pass snow ramp, watch for a moat-type gap — a short traverse beneath the snow edge may be needed to reach solid rock.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the short class 3–4 ridge step off the summit block back to the Point 5,841 pass, then descend the steep snow ramp below it facing in, plunge-stepping or self-belaying with an ice axe (a controlled glissade may be possible lower down if the snow is soft and the runout is clean and known — check before committing). From the base of the ramp, work back down through talus and boulders, staying climber's-right where possible to avoid the loosest scree, drop into the timber, and downclimb the brushy salmonberry/currant gully back to the cliff band. Pick a descending line through the boulder field to the river and re-ford to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — there is no fixed rappel station or bolted anchor on this route, and the discipline (scrambling, not roped climbing) is consistent with that. In icy or wet conditions some parties might choose to build a single natural rappel (sling around a horn or tree) to protect the short class 4 step just above the pass, but that is a judgment call, not standard practice for the route. Note there is a separate, much harder roped North Ridge line on this peak (1971 first ascent by Williamson/Oas/Bucher, three leads of 5th-class granite) that is a distinct technical route from this scramble line and should not be confused with it.
hazards: loose rock
trailless approach
river ford
steep snow / possible moat near summit pass

waysIn.name: Middle Fork ford and the north-side gully
waysIn.notes: Do not follow the maintained trail out of the road-end lot. Walk roughly 300 ft upstream and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to its true-right bank; in early summer this runs thigh-deep and cold, so scout upstream for a braided section or a log rather than forcing the main channel. Everything above is trailless: a boulder field, a brushy gully, timber, and open talus, with nearly all the day's gain packed into the last two miles. There is no water once you leave the river apart from occasional snowmelt trickles near the pass.
hazards: Cold, pushy river ford at the very start
Sustained salmonberry and black currant bushwhack in the lower gully
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Firm, sustained snow ramp below the pass — genuine self-arrest terrain
Moat between snow and rock near the top of the ramp

name: Standard Scramble
approach: From the Barlow Pass trailhead (2,360 ft, pavement's end on the Mountain Loop Highway) the climb starts with roughly 4 miles of the old Monte Cristo townsite road — closed to cars, open to bikes and foot traffic — following the South Fork Sauk River to the Monte Cristo townsite (~2,800 ft); most parties bike this stretch (about an hour each way) to save legs for the scramble. Rack the bike at the bike rack under the trees in the townsite, walk through the old town, and cross the footbridge to pick up signs for the Glacier Basin Trail. The trail climbs steadily along Glacier Creek, passing a prominent waterfall (Glacier Basin Falls) before leveling into Glacier Basin proper around 4,500-5,000 ft — a good water source and, in early season, still holding patchwork snow. In the basin, find a safe spot to ford the creek (can be a wade during high snowmelt) and locate a large boulder (~15 ft) that marks the start of the scramble proper; from there head toward a second, larger boulder (~20 ft) across the basin and ascend a blown-out gully streaked reddish with old mine tailings, working up the rib between two gullies. Roughly 25 ft below a headwall with a small waterfall, exit the gully to climber's left onto a band of red rock, traverse ledges up through scrub trees and brush, and pick up a faint climbers' path that switchbacks to the ridge crest around 5,500 ft. Follow the ridge (loose in spots, easy route-finding) to about 6,500 ft, where a distinctive "hobbit-like" rock feature marks a sharp left turn onto a loose talus traverse below the rock and out to the summit ridge. Hazards: creek crossing in Glacier Basin can be swift and cold during snowmelt; the mine-tailings gully and upper talus are loose and rockfall-prone, especially with parties above; early-season attempts (typically into July) cross avalanche-prone snow slopes and require ice axe and crampons. Head toward Ray's Knoll, the prominent hummock in the middle of Glacier Basin, before starting up the mine-tailings gully.
descent: Descend the same southwest ridge / west face line used on ascent — this is a scramble with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). From the summit block, downclimb back onto the ridge and locate the class 3 ledge that cuts back across the rock rib (it looks like a dead end at first; many parties mark it with a duck or cairn on the way up specifically to find it again on descent) — this leads back down to the loose talus traverse and around the "hobbit rock" at ~6,500 ft. Continue down the ridge to ~5,500 ft, then drop back through the brush/ledges band into the gully system. Rather than re-descending directly through the blown-out mine-tailings gully, stay skier's right to avoid steep cedar brush at the cost of a little mild bushwhacking, then rejoin the boulder landmarks back down into Glacier Basin. From the basin, re-ford the creek, retrace the Glacier Basin Trail past the waterfall to the Monte Cristo townsite, and bike/walk the old townsite road back out to Barlow Pass. Watch for loose rock and route-finding errors on the ridge/gully descent (easy to end up cliffed-out in the wrong gully), and for lingering snow/avalanche exposure on early-season descents — an ice axe (and crampons if snow is firm) is standard through early-mid summer.
hazards: long Monte Cristo approach
steep snow gullies early
afternoon thunderstorms
crux cliff band route-finding at ~6,500 ft
washed-out bridge / creek crossings near Monte Cristo townsite and on the Glacier Basin trail

waysIn.name: Glacier Basin: the mine-tailing streak across the creek
waysIn.notes: Ride or walk the gated Monte Cristo road from Barlow Pass to the townsite, rack the bike under the trees, cross the footbridge and take the Glacier Basin Trail up alongside Glacier Creek past the falls. Roughly 1.8 miles above the townsite, at about 4,400 ft, the creek flattens out among house-sized boulders; this is where the scramble starts. Ford the creek here — a genuine wade during snowmelt — and climb the rib between the two gullies on Cadet's southwest flank, using cairns and occasional flagging once the maintained tread is gone. The rib gains the ridge crest near 5,400 to 5,500 ft, after which you stay on or close to the crest. Higher up there is a second trap worth knowing before you set out: at about 6,300 ft, look up at the wide dark cliff band that sits at exactly 6,500 ft. A good-looking notch straight above you is where most people go wrong, and enough have done it that a well-defined trail leads to it. The line is roughly a hundred yards left, marked by a blocky gendarme standing up on the band — more visible the higher you get — with a deep, scary-looking gully a further seventy-five yards left again; the route is the ridge just inches right of that big gully. Cross below the gendarme, then look up for a small, short, exposed ledge.
hazards: The Glacier Basin creek ford is swift and cold during snowmelt
The tailings gully and the upper talus are loose and rockfall-prone with parties above
Avalanche-prone snow slopes on early-season attempts into July
The cliff band and the deep gully beside it are invisible from above — note how you got through before going higher
Three summits on this peak, and the maps have argued about which is highest

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 8 miles, then turn left onto the signed, gravel Eightmile Road. Cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large parking area at the road's end (passing the Eightmile Creek Trailhead en route). Northwest Forest Pass required.
descent: From the summit, head to Prusik Pass and follow the standard route's trail through the Upper Enchantment Basin, down Aasgard Pass, and down the Mountaineer Creek/Colchuck Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a demanding ~15-mile loop with sustained class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking on the ascent, requiring at least 12 hours car-to-car and an early start.
hazards: Sustained loose rock (class 3) on the ridge crest and especially on the traverse below the ridge towers.
No fixed protection or rappel stations anywhere on the route.
Early-season snow and ice on the ridge crest and in the Coney Lake basin.

waysIn.name: Eightmile trailhead and the burned slopes to the northeast ridge crest
waysIn.season: Mid to late summer, once the snow is off the ridge and out of the ground around Coney Lake
waysIn.notes: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road about eight miles, then turn left onto the signed gravel Eightmile Road, cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large lot at the road end. A Northwest Forest Pass is required. This route starts from the Stuart Lake trailhead lot at the road end, the same lot used for Colchuck Lake. The route climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to gain the ridge crest, then follows and traverses beneath the crest, and finishes with a talus gully and a short scramble to the summit block. It is described as an ascent route only. Most parties come down the other side of the mountain instead — Prusik Pass, the Upper Enchantment basin, down Aasgard Pass and out via Colchuck Lake to the Stuart Lake trailhead — which makes this a demanding roughly fifteen-mile loop with sustained Class 3 and bushwhacking, at least twelve hours car to car, and it finishes back at the same lot it started from, so no car shuttle is needed.
hazards: Steep, bushy, loose burned slopes with no trail on the lower half
A third of a mile of loose traversing below a band of unclimbable towers — the crux of the route
Sustained Class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking over a roughly fifteen-mile day
Descent is over the summit and out via Aasgard Pass and Colchuck Lake, a long way round back to the same trailhead
At least twelve hours car to car, so an early start is not optional
Snow lingering around Coney Lake and on the ridge in early summer

name: Northwest Ridge
approach: From the Stuart Lake trailhead (about 3,400 ft; Northwest Forest Pass) take the Stuart Lake trail about 1.25 miles to just before the Mountaineer Creek bridge, then leave the trail and go up west and south through open forest.
descent: Most parties retrace the route; a longer alternative heads east across the Druid Plateau, over Prusik Pass, through the Enchantments and down Aasgard Pass.
hazards: steep brush and slide alder low on the mountain
snow and ice on the upper ridge into July
exposed friction slab at the summit, dangerous when wet or icy

name: South Slopes
approach: Start at the Snow Lakes Trailhead (paved, day-use permit required, ~4 miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth). Follow the Snow Lakes Trail (#1553) as it climbs through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, passing Nada and Snow Lakes (roughly 6-7 miles in) before continuing up into the core Enchantment Lakes basin — Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun Lake, Sprite Lake, and Perfection Lake. By the time you reach Perfection Lake you have covered on the order of 10-11 miles and about 6,000 ft of gain from the trailhead, all on maintained but rocky, sometimes eroded tread with several creek crossings that can run high with snowmelt in early season. At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the climbers'/scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass (~7,463 ft) — this junction is easy to miss and is the last reliable water before the cross-country section. From Prusik Pass the route leaves all trail: contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, staying on the left (west) side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then continue north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft, turn northwest and climb steep talus/scree (snow-covered into mid-summer) up onto the Druid Plateau (~8,350 ft), where Cannon's summit block comes into view across the plateau. Cross the plateau and take the western slopes to the base of the summit block; the final ~15 ft to the true summit is a low-angle but exposed friction slab climbed via a ramp on the block's south side, with almost no positive holds — approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference here. Because the round trip from the trailhead is roughly 30+ miles with 7,300+ ft of gain, essentially all parties camp in or near the core Enchantment zone (competitive overnight permits required in season) rather than attempting it car-to-car; treat the whole cross-country section above Prusik Pass as serious route-finding terrain with no cairns or tread, frequently holding snow into July, and exposed to sun/lightning with no bail-out shelter.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the exposed friction-slab ramp off the summit block (often the psychological crux of the day, since downclimbing low-angle slab is harder to read than ascending it), cross back over the Druid Plateau, and pick your way back down the talus/scree slopes to the rib at ~7,900-8,000 ft. From there reverse the contouring traverse at 7,300-7,400 ft past the Lorelei Lakelets to Prusik Pass, then drop back down the scrambler's path to Perfection Lake and rejoin the maintained Snow Lakes Trail for the long hike out past Sprite, Leprechaun, and Viviane Lakes, Snow Lakes, and down to the trailhead. This is a pure scramble/downclimb with no fixed rappel anchors on the standard South Slopes line — no rope or rappel gear is needed for typical summer conditions, though some parties carry a short rope/sling for confidence on the summit block slab. The main descent hazards are the same as the approach in reverse: losing the faint route back to Prusik Pass in whiteout or dusk, loose talus on the plateau slopes, and lingering snow/verglass on the slab or upper gullies in early season, which has turned some ascents into technical downclimbs requiring crampons and careful footwork on rock. A minority of strong parties link Cannon into a longer Enchantments traverse (continuing on to McClellan Peak or exiting via Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake) rather than reversing to Snow Lakes, but that is a route variation, not the standard descent.
hazards: loose talus and scree on the slopes
route-finding through benches and brush
cliffing out on descent
afternoon thunderstorms
a steep, often snow-filled gully below Druid Plateau on the north-slope (Coney Lake) approach that can hold snow into July

waysIn.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered ten or eleven miles and about 6,000 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the west side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
hazards: No cairns or tread above Prusik Pass: serious route-finding over talus and heather
Steep talus and scree up to the Druid Plateau, loose underfoot
Snow lingering on the cross-country section into July; verglas on shaded ground
Final fifteen feet are an exposed, holdless friction slab, harder to downclimb than climb
No shelter on open high ground: sun, lightning and afternoon storms
Very long approach (30+ miles round trip, 7,300+ ft gain) so nearly everyone camps

waysIn.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
waysIn.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail at all
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain; landmarks of the other approach do not apply
Steep gully below the plateau can hold snow into July; verglas on shaded ground
Exposed, holdless friction ramp on the summit block, harder to downclimb
No shelter on high ground: lightning and afternoon storms
Loose talus and scree on the slopes; benches can cliff out on descent
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you want much less distance than the Snow Lakes walk and can handle a full day of brushy, trail-less navigation with cliff bands.

name: Northwest Couloir–North Ridge
approach: Reached via the North Fork Entiat Trail to Saska Basin and Saska Pass, commonly combined with ascents of Saska Peak, Emerald Peak, and Pinnacle Mountain on the same trip rather than as a dedicated single-peak approach. In late June the first three or four miles of the North Fork valley run through burnt forest with many fallen trees, and snow covers the trail between about 6,600 and 6,900 ft.
hazards: Lingering snow/verglas on the north ridge creating route-finding and exposure hazards later in the season than expected

name: Southeast Slopes
approach: From the end of FR-5606 (the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, ~3,940 ft), pick up the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. This lower section sits outside wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal and commonly used to knock out easy miles. The first ~6 miles follow the North Fork Entiat River on a gentle, mostly forested grade, with the river itself as a reliable water source the whole way — top off here, since the route runs dry above. Some post-wildfire sections have significant blowdown; a few parties describe losing the tread briefly among downed timber and having to scramble back onto it. At about mile 6.1 a signed spur splits off to Fern Lake (Trail #1436) — stay on #1437. Around mile 7, at roughly 5,800 ft, the main trail bends sharply east and climbs switchbacks for about a half mile to a junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 at about 6,600 ft, roughly a mile southwest of Cardinal's summit and a useful timing landmark. The final approach mile above this junction is noted as steep and loose underfoot. From the open meadow/basin past the junction, leave the trail and hike east through sparse forest, then talus, toward Cardinal's west/southwest flank. For the Southeast Slopes line specifically, contour or drop onto the peak's western slopes and work south below the summit ridge across steep talus and scree to reach the gully leading to the notch between the north and middle (traditionally climbed) summits — the same scree-gully notch most parties use regardless of which flank they approach from. Loose rock is constant in the upper basin and gully, so a helmet is worthwhile and parties should avoid stacking up directly below one another. Round trip to the summit runs roughly 20-21 miles with about 4,700 ft of gain, so most parties do it as a long single day or a one-night backpack with camp in the meadows/basin below the peak. The trail crosses Grouse Creek on a log partway up, within one of the fire-damaged sections that has blowdown.
descent: This is a walk-down/downclimb — no rope work or anchors are needed on the Southeast Slopes line. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose scree gully from the notch back into the upper basin, then pick your way back down through talus and sparse forest to rejoin the North Fork Entiat Trail near the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction (~6,600 ft). From there it's a straightforward trail descent down the switchbacks to about 5,800 ft and out along the gentle lower six-plus miles back to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead. The scree gully is the main descent hazard — it's loose top to bottom, so descend deliberately, keep the group tight, and stay alert for rockfall triggered by climbers above. One trip report on this peak noted the descent taking roughly half the time of the ascent once back on established trail. No rappels are required on this route.
hazards: long, remote multi-day approach with poor cell coverage
routefinding on open talus and in the gully above camp
exposed, sometimes-corniced summit ridge traverse (~500 ft of consequence)
steep snow (40–50°) in the gully through June
Grouse Creek log crossing and fire-related blowdown on the lower trail

waysIn.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the west-side basin
waysIn.season: Late May-Sep. In late May and June this is effectively a snow climb — the gully to the saddle holds 40-50 degree snow and wants an axe and crampons. By August it dries into loose Class 3 talus
waysIn.notes:
From the end of FR-5606 at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,940 ft, take North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. The lower trail is outside the wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal on the first several miles and many parties use one on a 20-mile round trip.

The first six miles follow the river on a gentle forested grade, straight through old burn. The river is the last reliable water — everything above is dry — so fill before leaving the valley. Expect to work over, under and around blowdown, and to lose the tread briefly among downed timber; Grouse Creek is crossed on a log inside one of the worst of those stretches.

A signed spur to Fern Lake splits off at about mile 6.1 — stay on #1437. Around mile 7 near 5,800 ft the trail bends sharply east and switchbacks about half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 junction near 6,600 ft. That junction is a useful timing landmark: the summit is roughly a mile from it.

Leave the trail there and head east through sparse forest and then talus toward the peak's west and south-west flank. A camp flat sits around 7,100 ft in the open basin.
hazards: A gully that is loose top to bottom in summer and 40-50 degree snow through June, with the whole party in the fall line
An exposed, sometimes-corniced summit ridge traverse of roughly 500 ft with genuine consequence
A short unrated technical step between the middle summit and the true south summit that many parties decline
Constant loose rock on the traverse below the summit ridge, so parties must not stack up
A dry, long approach through burn with heavy blowdown, and no water above the valley

name: Carne Mountain Trail
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of FR 6211), start on the wide, gently graded Phelps Creek Trail #1511 heading north/upstream along Phelps Creek through open forest. In roughly 0.25–0.4 mile, watch for a signed junction and bear right (steeply uphill) onto the narrower Carne Mountain Trail — this is the last easy water for a while, so top off here or at the small creeklet just past the junction, since the climb above is essentially dry except for early-season snowmelt. From the junction the trail wastes no time, switchbacking up through open forest, vine maple, and beargrass slopes and gaining about 2,600 ft in the next 2.9 miles — a sustained, steep grade with little flat respite. Around 3.1–3.2 miles from the trailhead you top out at a broad saddle near 6,800 ft with a sweeping view of Mount Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, Clark Mountain, and Glacier Peak; this saddle is also the junction with the climbers'/unmaintained Rock Creek Trail heading east. From the saddle, bear left and switchback up open talus and scree for a final 0.4–0.5 mile to the summit at 7,091 ft, passing near a minor false high point along the way. The standard route is Class 1–2 the entire way (a steep trail/talus walk, no technical scrambling), but snow can linger on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early-mid July, and the exposed saddle/ridge can be windy — an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season snow patches near the top. There is no ford of Phelps Creek on this route (the trail junction is well before any major crossing); the only route-finding subtlety is picking the correct fork at the Phelps Creek/Carne Mountain junction low down and staying on-trail through the talus near the summit block.
descent: This is a walk-off — reverse the ascent trail all the way back to the Phelps Creek Trailhead. No rappelling or technical downclimbing is involved on the standard route; the only care needed is on the steep upper switchbacks and talus near the saddle if snow or loose scree is present, and general Class 2 talus-walking care on the final push off the summit. Parties wanting a longer, more strenuous alternative descent (or ascent) can instead traverse east from the 6,800-ft saddle past Point 7103 toward Ice Lakes and drop into Leroy Basin, following Leroy Creek's trail back down to the Phelps Creek Trail and out — but that loop adds significant mileage and about 1,200 ft more cumulative gain (roughly 16 mi / 4,800 ft total versus the ~7.3 mi / 3,600 ft standard out-and-back), so it is a distinct high-route variant rather than the default descent.
hazards: steep switchbacks
early-season snow on the upper trail

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek Trail to the Carne Mountain Trail #1508 fork
waysIn.season: Mid-July through October. Snow lingers on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early or mid July, and the larch display peaks in late September and early October.
waysIn.notes: From the road-end lot at the top of the Phelps Creek Road spur, the trail leaving the parking area is the wide, nearly level Phelps Creek Trail #1511 heading north up-valley through open forest — which is not what the rest of the day looks like. A quarter to four-tenths of a mile along it, a signed junction sends the narrower Carne Mountain Trail #1508 steeply uphill to the right. Fill water at the fork or at the small creeklet just past it, because everything above is dry apart from early-season snowmelt. The trail then switchbacks up through open forest, vine maple and beargrass with very little flat ground until it breaks out into a small cirque holding campsites and a stream, then climbs past a faint junction at a low pass to a broad saddle on the ridge.
hazards: Sustained steep grade with essentially no water above the low fork
Snow lingering on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early or mid July, worth carrying an axe for
The saddle and summit ridge are exposed to wind
Loose talus and scree on the final switchbacks below the summit block
